problem: 7. Circles $\omega$ and $\Omega$ touch externally at point $F$, and their common external tangent touches circles $\omega$ and $\Omega$ at points $A$ and $B$, respectively. Line $\ell$ passes through point $B$, intersects circle $\Omega$ again at point $C$, and intersects $\omega$ at points $D$ and $E$ (point $D$ is between $C$ and $E$). The common tangent of the circles passing through point $F$ intersects lines $A B$ and $B E$ at points $P$ and $H$, respectively (point $H$ lies between points $P$ and $F$). It is known that $B C=60$, $D H=H C=2$. Find the length of segment $H P$ and the radii of both circles.
solution:
Answer: $H P=8 \sqrt{31}, r=6 \sqrt{\frac{93}{5}}, R=2 \sqrt{465}$.

Solution. We apply the theorem of the tangent and the secant three times:

$$
\begin{gathered}
H F^{2}=H C \cdot H B=2 \cdot 62 \Rightarrow H F=2 \sqrt{31} \\
H F^{2}=H D \cdot H E \Rightarrow H E=\frac{H F^{2}}{H D}=62 \\
B A^{2}=B D \cdot B E=64 \cdot 124=\Rightarrow B A=16 \sqrt{31}
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the segments of the tangents drawn from a point to a circle are equal to each other, $P F=P A=P B$, therefore, $P F=\frac{1}{2} A B=8 \sqrt{31}$. Thus, $P H=P F-F H=6 \sqrt{31}$. Let $\angle B P H=\gamma$. Then, by the cosine theorem for triangle $B P H$, we get $B H^{2}=B P^{2}+H P^{2}-2 B P \cdot P H \cdot \cos \gamma$, i.e., $62^{2}=64 \cdot 31+36 \cdot 31-2 \cdot 6 \cdot 8 \cdot 31 \cos \gamma$, from which $31=16+9-24 \cos \gamma, \cos \gamma=-\frac{1}{4}$.

Let $O$ and $Q$ be the centers, and $R$ and $r$ be the radii of circles $\Omega$ and $\omega$ respectively; since the circles are tangent, the point of tangency $F$ lies on the line of centers $O Q$, and $O Q \perp P H$. Angles $B$ and $F$ of quadrilateral $O B P F$ are right angles, so $\angle B O F=180^{\circ}-\angle B P F=180^{\circ}-\gamma$.

Consider the right trapezoid $A B O Q$. In it, $O Q=R+r, O B=R, A Q=r, A B=16 \sqrt{31}$, $\angle B O Q=180^{\circ}-\gamma$. Dropping a perpendicular $Q H$ from point $Q$ to the base $B O$, we get a right triangle $O H Q$, in which $Q H=A B=16 \sqrt{31}, O H=R-r$. By the Pythagorean theorem, we get
$(R+r)^{2}=(R-r)^{2}+(16 \sqrt{31})^{2}$; moreover, $\frac{1}{4}=\cos \left(180^{\circ}-\gamma\right)=\frac{R-r}{R+r}$. From the last equation, we get $R=\frac{5 r}{3}$, and from the first, it follows that $R r=64 \cdot 31$. Solving this system of equations, we find that $R=8 \sqrt{\frac{155}{3}}, r=8 \sqrt{\frac{93}{5}}$.

problem: 11-2. In a certain coordinate system, the graph of the function $y=\cos ^{2} x$ was plotted. After that, the coordinate axes were erased. Construct a coordinate system so that the same line becomes the graph of the function $z=\cos t$ in the new coordinate system.
solution:
Solution. We have $y=\cos ^{2} x=\frac{1+\cos 2 x}{2}$. We can now set $2 x=t, y=(z+1) / 2$, then the variables $z$ and $t$ are related by $z=\cos t$, meaning the pair $(t, z)$ defines the position of a point in the desired coordinate system.

We see that $t=0$ when $x=0$, and $t=1$ when $x=2$. This means that the scale on the $x$-axis has been halved, while the origin remains at the same level.

On the other hand, the value $z=0$ (the origin) corresponds to $y=1 / 2$, and the value $z=1$ corresponds to the coordinate $y=1$. Thus, the scale on the $O y$-axis has also been halved, but the axis has shifted up by $1 / 2$ (in terms of the old coordinate system).

problem: 2. In the plane, a segment $A V$ and an acute angle of size $\alpha$ are given. Determine the set of centers of circumcircles of all triangles $A B C$ with an internal angle $\alpha$ at vertex $A$, whose altitudes intersect at point $V$.
solution:
SOLUTION. First, let's prove a generally useful statement about the intersection $V$ of the altitudes of any acute triangle $ABC$. Let $V'$ be the intersection of the line containing the altitude $CC_0$ with the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ (Fig. 1). The right triangles $C_0VA$ and $A_0VC$ are similar (they also share the angle at vertex $V$), so $\left|\nless BAA_0\right| = \left|\Varangle BCC_0\right|$. The angles $BCC_0$ and $V'AB$ are congruent inscribed angles subtending the arc $V'B$, so points $V$ and $V'$ are symmetric with respect to the line $AB$.

If we denote the angles of triangle $ABC$ in the usual way, then $\left|\nless ACV'\right| = \left|\Varangle ACC_0\right| = 90^\circ - \alpha$, so for the length of segment $AV$, due to the mentioned symmetry, we get

$$
|AV| = \left|AV'\right| = 2r \sin \left(90^\circ - \alpha\right) = 2r \cos \alpha,
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the circumcircle $k$ of triangle $ABC$ (and also of triangle $AV'C$). The same formula (1) applies to triangle $ABC$ with an acute internal angle $\alpha$ at vertex $A$ even if one of the other two internal angles (e.g., at vertex $B$) is right or obtuse (Fig. 2). The entire reasoning can be repeated word for word.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_04_17_0d6c7c8c0a751990c7fdg-02.jpg?height=586&width=548&top_left_y=1963&top_left_x=754)

Fig. 1

Now we will tackle the competition problem with the given points $A, V$ and the given size of the acute angle $\alpha$. Formula (1) leads us to the conclusion that the circumcircles of all considered triangles $ABC$ will have the same radius

$$
r = \frac{|AV|}{2 \cos \alpha}
$$

thus their centers $O$ will be at a fixed, precisely determined distance $r$ from the given point $A$. However, it is necessary to determine which part of the circle $l(A, r)$ the centers $O$ will fill; it will certainly be a set symmetric with respect to the line $AV$, because the symmetry $s$ with axis $AV$ transforms a suitable triangle into a suitable triangle. For this purpose, we will express the size of the angle $VAO$ in terms of the internal angles $\beta = |\Varangle ABC|$ and $\gamma = |\Varangle ACB|$. We will assume that $\beta \geqq \gamma$ (in the opposite case, the labels of vertices $B, C$ can be swapped from the very beginning).

First, assume that $\beta < 90^\circ$, so triangle $ABC$ is acute and we can work with Fig. 1 again. From the isosceles triangle $ABO$ with the internal angle $2\gamma$ at the main vertex $O$, we see that $|\Varangle BAO| = 90^\circ - \gamma$, and from the right triangle $BAA_0$ we get $|\Varangle BAV| = 90^\circ - \beta$. Since both points $O, V$ lie in the half-plane $ABC$, we get for the angle $VAO$ the expression

$$
|\nless VAO| = |\nless BAO| - |\nless BAV| = (90^\circ - \gamma) - (90^\circ - \beta) = \beta - \gamma
$$

(remember that $\beta \geqq \gamma$).
In the case $\beta \geqq 90^\circ$ according to Fig. 2, similarly we find that $|\nless BAO| = 90^\circ - \gamma$ and $|\nless BAV| = \beta - 90^\circ$, so

$$
|\Varangle VAO| = |\Varangle BAO| + |\Varangle BAV| = (90^\circ - \gamma) + (\beta - 90^\circ) = \beta - \gamma.
$$

We see that $|\nless VAO| = \beta - \gamma$ regardless of whether triangle $ABC$ is acute, right, or obtuse.

Now we can easily complete the solution of the problem: from the derived size of the angle $VAO$ we get the estimate

$$
|\Varangle VAO| = \beta - \gamma < \beta + \gamma = 180^\circ - \alpha,
$$

so the point $O$ lies inside the arc of the circle $l(A, r)$ determined by the inequality

$$
|\Varangle VAO| < 180^\circ - \alpha.
$$

If we choose an angle $\varepsilon, 0^\circ \leqq \varepsilon < 180^\circ - \alpha$, we can easily calculate what the internal angles $\beta$ and $\gamma$ must be to satisfy $|\Varangle VAO| = \varepsilon$:

$$
\beta = \frac{180^\circ - \alpha + \varepsilon}{2}, \quad \gamma = \frac{180^\circ - \alpha - \varepsilon}{2}.
$$

If we inscribe a helper triangle $A'B'C'$ in any circle of radius $r$ from formula (2) with the given angle $\alpha$ at vertex $A'$ and the calculated angles $\beta, \gamma$ at vertices $B'$ and $C'$ respectively, for its orthocenter $V'$ and the center $O'$ of the circumcircle, the equalities $\left|A'V'\right| = |AV|$ and $\left|\nless V'A'O'\right| = \varepsilon$ will be satisfied. In a congruent transformation that maps segment $A'V'$ to segment $AV$, the triangle $A'B'C'$ will transform into a suitable triangle $ABC$, whose center $O$ of the circumcircle will lie on the circle $l$ and satisfy the equality $\left|\nless V'A'O'\right| = \varepsilon$.

Conclusion. The sought set of centers $O$ of the circumcircles is the arc of the circle with center $A$ and radius $r = \frac{1}{2}|AV| / \cos \alpha$ determined by the inequality $|\nless VAO| < 180^\circ - \alpha$ (the endpoints of this arc do not belong to the resulting set, Fig. 3).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_04_17_0d6c7c8c0a751990c7fdg-04.jpg?height=734&width=685&top_left_y=1786&top_left_x=617)

Fig. 3

SUPPLEMENTARY AND ADDITIONAL PROBLEMS:

N1. Show that two lines, on which the bisectors of the internal angles (or altitudes, or lines connecting the vertices with the center of the circumcircle) of a triangle lie, form an angle whose size depends only on the size of the internal angle at the remaining vertex. Does such a statement hold for the lines on which the medians of the triangle lie?

N2. Prove that the points symmetric to the orthocenter of an acute triangle with respect to the lines on which the sides of the triangle lie lie on the circumcircle of the triangle. [See the solution of the competition problem.] Derive from this an interesting statement about three circles, which are images of the circumcircle in the mentioned three axial symmetries. [These three circles pass through one point, namely the orthocenter.]

N3. Express the distances from the orthocenter of an acute triangle to its vertices in terms of the cosines of its internal angles and the radius of the circumcircle. [See the solution of the competition problem.]

D1. Show that from problem N2 the same statement follows for an obtuse triangle by the following reasoning: if $V$ is the orthocenter of triangle $ABC$ with an obtuse angle at vertex $C$, then point $C$ is the orthocenter of the acute triangle $ABV$.

problem:
Find all triples of positive integers $(a, b, p)$ with $p$ prime and 
$$ a^{p}=b!+p $$ 
(Belgium)
solution:
Clearly, $a>1$. We consider three cases. Case 1: We have $ab$ which is also impossible since in this case we have $b! \leqslant a!a > 1$. Case 2: We have $a > p$. In this case $b! = a^{p} - p > p^{p} - p \geqslant p!$ so $b > p$ which means that $a^{p} = b! + p$ is divisible by $p$. Hence, $a$ is divisible by $p$ and $b! = a^{p} - p$ is not divisible by $p^{2}$. This means that $b(2 p - 1)! + p \geqslant b! + p$. Comment. The inequality $p^{2 p} > (2 p - 1)! + p$ can be shown e.g. by using 
$$ (2 p - 1)! = [1 \cdot (2 p - 1)] \cdot [2 \cdot (2 p - 2)] \cdots \cdots [(p - 1)(p + 1)] \cdot pp$$ ! and so $b \geqslant p + 1$ which implies that $v_{2}((p + 1)!) \leqslant v_{2}(b!) = v_{2}\left(p^{p-1} - 1\right) \stackrel{L T E}{=} 2 v_{2}(p - 1) + v_{2}(p + 1) - 1 = v_{2}\left(\frac{p - 1}{2} \cdot (p - 1) \cdot (p + 1)\right)$, where in the middle we used lifting-the-exponent lemma. On the RHS we have three factors of $(p + 1)!$. But, due to $p + 1 \geqslant 8$, there are at least 4 even numbers among $1, 2, \ldots, p + 1$, so this case is not possible.

problem:
3. Two two-digit numbers are written on the board. Andrey multiplied them, getting a four-digit number with the first digit 2. Pasha added them and got a three-digit number. If the first digit is erased from Andrey's number, Pasha's number is obtained. What numbers were written?

(l. S. Korechkova)
solution:
Solution. If the numbers $x$ and $y$ were recorded, then by the condition $xy = 2000 + x + y$, which means $xy - x - y + 1 = 2001$, or $(x-1)(y-1) = 2001$. Since $2001 = 3 \cdot 23 \cdot 29$ and $x, y$ are two-digit numbers, then $x-1$ and $y-1$ can be $23, 29, 23 \cdot 3$ or $29 \cdot 3$. Therefore, $x, y \in \{24, 30, 70, 88\}$. The pairs that satisfy the condition are $\{24, 88\}$ and $\{30, 70\}$.

problem:
1. In a math test, $N<40$ people participate. The passing score is set at 65. The test results are as follows: the average score of all participants is 66, that of the promoted is 71, and that of the failed is 56. However, due to an error in the formulation of a question, all scores are increased by 5. At this point, the average score of the promoted becomes 75 and that of the non-promoted 59.

(a) Find all possible values of $N$.

(b) Find all possible values of $N$ in the case where, after the increase, the average score of the promoted became 79 and that of the non-promoted 47.
solution:
Solution: (a) Let $P_{1}$ be the number of students who passed before the score increase, and $P_{2}$ be the number of students who passed after the score increase. From the information we have, we can write:

$$
66 N=71 P_{1}+56\left(N-P_{1}\right), \quad 71 N=75 P_{2}+59\left(N-P_{2}\right)
$$

From the first relation, solving the equations, we get $10 N=15 P_{1}$ or $2 N=3 P_{1}$, from which, since $N$ and $P_{1}$ are integers, we can conclude that $N$ is a multiple of 3. Similarly, from the second relation, we have $12 N=16 P_{2}$ or $3 N=4 P_{2}$, and thus $N$ is a multiple of 4. In conclusion, $N$ must be a multiple of 3 and 4, i.e., of 12, and can therefore be 12, 24, or 36. These three cases are indeed possible. Let's look for an example with $N=12$, trying to have scores as equal as possible. If 8 people, i.e., those who were immediately passing, had a score of 71 before the increase, one person got 62, and the remaining three got 54, we have verified all the assumptions of the problem. The cases $N=24$ and $N=36$ are analogous, respectively doubling and tripling the number of people in each score range.

(b) No $N$ can satisfy the conditions of this point. Let $M_{p}$ be the average score - before the increase - of those who were not passing before the increase but would pass after. Then we would have:

$$
76 P_{1}+\left(M_{p}+5\right)\left(P_{2}-P_{1}\right)=79 P_{2}
$$

But $M_{p}<65$, so $M_{p}+5<70<76$, from which

$$
79 P_{2}=76 P_{1}+\left(M_{p}+5\right)\left(P_{2}-P_{1}\right)<76 P_{1}+76\left(P_{2}-P_{1}\right)=76 P_{2}<79 P_{2}
$$

which is a contradiction.

problem:

Let the specified plane pass through the midpoints $M$ and $N$ of sides $AB$ and $AC$ of the base $ABC$ of a regular triangular pyramid $DABC$ and intersect the lateral edge $AD$ at point $P$, and the median $AF$ of the equilateral triangle $ABC$ at point $K$. The plane of triangle $ADF$ passes through the perpendicular $DO$ (the height of the pyramid) to the plane of the base $ABC$. Therefore, the plane $ADF$ is perpendicular to the plane of the base of the pyramid. The intersecting plane is also perpendicular to the plane of the base of the pyramid (by condition) and intersects the plane $ADF$ along the line $PK$. Thus, the line $PK$ is perpendicular to the plane of the base of the pyramid and $KP \parallel DO$. Further, we have:

$$

AK=\frac{1}{2} AF, \quad AO=\frac{2}{3} AF, \quad \frac{AK}{AO}=\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} AF}{AF}=\frac{3}{1} \\
KP=\frac{\partial D \cdot AK}{AC}=\frac{13}{1}=3, \quad MN=\frac{1}{2} BC=1
\end{gathered}
$$

Since $KP$ is the height of triangle $MPN$, we have

$$
S_{\triangle MPN}=\frac{1}{2} MN \cdot KP=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 1 \cdot 3=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

problem: Example 3 Given positive integers $k, l$. Find all functions $f: \mathbf{Z}_{+} \rightarrow \mathbf{Z}_{+}$, such that for any $m, n \in \mathbf{Z}_{+}$, we have $(f(m)+f(n)) \mid (m+n+l)^{k}$.
solution:
【Analysis】First, when $l$ is odd, take $m=n$, we have
$$
2 f(m) \mid(2 m+l)^{k},
$$

which is obviously a contradiction.
Therefore, when $l$ is odd, there does not exist a function $f$ that satisfies the condition.
Next, we discuss the case when $l$ is even.
We still conjecture that $f(n)=n+\frac{l}{2}$.
To do this, we first prove a lemma.
Lemma For any $m \in \mathbf{Z}_{+}$, we have
$$
f(m+1)-f(m)= \pm 1 \text {. }
$$

Proof Clearly, $f$ is not a constant function.
If $|f(m+1)-f(m)| \neq 1$, then there exists a prime $p$,
such that
$$
p \mid(f(m+1)-f(m)) .
$$

Take $e$ such that $p^{\circ}>m+l$. Combining the condition, we have
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\left(f\left(p^{e}-m-l\right)+f(m)\right) \mid\left(p^{e}-m-l+m+l\right)^{k} \\
\Rightarrow\left(f\left(p^{e}-m-l\right)+f(m)\right) \mid p^{e k} . \\
\text { Also, } f\left(p^{e}-m-l\right)+f(m) \geqslant 1+1=2, \text { so } \\
p \mid\left(f\left(p^{e}-m-1\right)+f(m)\right) .
\end{array}
$$

By the assumption, we get
$$
\begin{array}{l}
p \mid\left(f\left(p^{e}-m-1\right)+f(m+1)\right) . \\
\text { And }\left(f\left(p^{e}-m-1\right)+f(m+1)\right) \mid\left(p^{e}+1\right)^{k},
\end{array}
$$

which is clearly a contradiction.
The lemma is proved.
By the lemma, we have
$$
f(n) \leqslant f(n-1)+1 \leqslant \cdots \leqslant f(1)+(n-1) \text {. }
$$

Next, choose a sufficiently large prime $p$, satisfying
$$
p>l+1, p^{2}>p+2 f(1)-l-2 \text {. }
$$

Notice,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
(f(1)+f(p-l-1)) \mid(p-l-1+l+1)^{k} \\
\Rightarrow\left(f(1)+f(p-l-1) \mid p^{k},\right. \\
q)$. Then $f(p-l-1)=p-f(1)$,
and $f(q-l-1)=q-f(1)$.
Thus, $p-f(1)=f(p-l-1)$
$\leqslant f(p-l-2)+1 \leqslant \cdots$
$\leqslant f(q-l-1)+(p-q)$
$=q-f(1)+(p-q)=p-f(1)$.
All equalities in the above expression hold, indicating that for $q \leqslant n \leqslant p$, we have
$f(n-l-1)=n-f(1)$.
In particular, for $n \geqslant q-l-1$, we have
$f(n)=n+l+1-f(1)=n+c$ (where $c$ is a constant).
Fix $n$, and choose
$$
q-l-1 \leqslant N \leqslant p-l-1,
$$

such that $n+N+l$ is a prime.
In fact, since $p$ is sufficiently large, we have
$(f(n)+f(N)) \mid(n+N+l)^{k}$
$\Rightarrow f(n)+f(N)=(n+N+l)^{e}(1 \leqslant e \leqslant k)$.
Also, $f(N)=N+c$, and as $N \rightarrow+\infty$, unless $e=1$, a contradiction will inevitably arise. Therefore,
$f(n)=n+l-c\left(n \in \mathbf{Z}_{+}\right)$.
Substituting into the condition of the problem, we get
$$
(m+n+2 l-2 c) \mid(m+n+l)^{k} \text {. }
$$

Then clearly,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
(m+n+2 l-2 c) \mid(m+n+l-(m+n+2 l-2 c))^{k} \\
\Rightarrow(m+n+2 l-2 c) \mid(2 c-l)^{k} .
\end{array}
$$

Taking $m \rightarrow+\infty, n \rightarrow+\infty$, the right side is a constant, which must be 0, i.e., $c=\frac{l}{2}$.
Therefore, when $l$ is even, $f(n)=n+\frac{l}{2}\left(n \in \mathbf{Z}_{+}\right)$; when $l$ is odd, there is no function $f$ that satisfies the condition.

problem: For the numbers $1000^{2}, 1001^{2}, 1002^{2}, \ldots$, the last two digits are discarded. How many of the first terms of the resulting sequence form an arithmetic progression?
solution:
The general term of the original sequence is: $a_{n}=\left(10^{3}+n\right)^{2}=10^{6}+2 n \cdot 10^{3}+n^{2}$ ( $a_{0}-$ the first term).

Let the general term of the resulting sequence be denoted by $b_{n}$, then

$b_{n}=\left[\frac{a_{n}}{100}\right]=\left[\frac{10^{6}+2 \cdot n \cdot 10^{3}+n^{2}}{100}\right]=10^{4}+20 n+\left[\frac{n^{2}}{100}\right]$

Therefore, the difference between consecutive terms of the new sequence will be 20 as long as
$\left[\frac{n^{2}}{100}\right]=0$, that is, if $n^{2}<100$. Considering that $n-$ is a natural number or zero, we get: $0 \leq n \leq 9$. Thus,

the first 10 terms of the new sequence form an arithmetic progression.

problem:
Let's assume that the birth of a girl and a boy is equally likely. It is known that a certain family has two children.

a) What is the probability that one is a boy and one is a girl?

b) It is additionally known that one of the children is a boy. What is the probability now that there is one boy and one girl in the family?

c) It is additionally known that the boy was born on a Monday. What is the probability now that there is one boy and one girl in the family?
solution:
a) Children appear in a certain sequence (MM, MD, DM, or DD). All sequences are equally likely, and the probability of each is 1/4. The condition "boy and girl" is favorable for two outcomes MD and DM, so the probability of this is $2: 4 = 1 / 2$.

b) Out of the four sequences, three remain equally likely: MM, MD, and DM. Therefore, the probability of the event "boy and girl" is now $2 / 3$.

c) Let's introduce the days of the week: $\mathrm{M}_{M}$ - a boy born on Monday, $\mathrm{M}_{O}$ - a boy born on another day of the week. According to the condition, five sequences are possible: $\mathrm{M}_{M} \mathrm{M}_{M}, \mathrm{M}_{M} \mathrm{M}_{O}$, $\mathrm{M}_{O} \mathrm{M}_{M}, \mathrm{M}_{M} D, D \mathrm{M}_{M}$

Considering that the probability of being born on a Monday is $1 / 7$, and on another day is $6 / 7$, we find that the total probability of the possible sequences is

$\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{7} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{7} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{7} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{6}{7} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{6}{7} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{7} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{7} \cdot \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{7} = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{27}{49}$.

Of these sequences, only two: $\mathrm{M}_{M} D$ and $D \mathrm{M}_{M}$ favor the event "boy and girl". Their total probability is $1 / 4 \cdot 2 / 7$.

Therefore, the conditional probability of the event "boy and girl" given the condition "there is a boy born on Monday" is $2 / 7 : 27 / 49 = 14 / 27$.

## Answer

a) $1 / 2 ;$ b) $2 / 3 ;$ c) $14 / 27$

$$

$$

The maximum value of the quadratic function $P$ is achieved at

$$
x=-\frac{5}{2 \cdot\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)}=\frac{10}{3} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad y=3-\frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{10}{3}=\frac{1}{2}

The maximum value of the quadratic function $P$ is

$$

(that is, $\left.P\left(\frac{10}{3}\right)=\frac{169}{3}\right)$.

The dimensions of the new plate are $12-x=12-\frac{10}{3}=\frac{26}{3} \mathrm{~cm}, 7-y=\frac{13}{2} \mathrm{~cm}$.

Analysis From $a_{n+1}=\frac{3^{n+1} a_{n}}{a_{n}+3^{n+1}}$, we know that $\frac{1}{a_{n+1}}=\frac{a_{n}+3^{n+1}}{3^{n+1} a_{n}}=\frac{1}{a_{n}}+\frac{1}{3^{n+1}}$.
$$
\frac{1}{a_{n}}=\frac{1}{a_{1}}+\left(\frac{1}{a_{2}}-\frac{1}{a_{1}}\right)+\cdots+\left(\frac{1}{a_{n}}-\frac{1}{a_{n-1}}\right)=\frac{1}{3}+\left(\frac{1}{3^{2}}+\frac{1}{3^{3}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{3^{n}}\right)=\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1-\frac{1}{3^{n}}}{1-\frac{1}{3}}=\frac{3^{n}-1}{2 \cdot 3^{n}}
$$

Thus, $a_{n}=\frac{2 \cdot 3^{n}}{3^{n}-1}$, so the answer is $a_{n}=\frac{2 \cdot 3^{n}}{3^{n}-1}$.

1.11. a) The golden section refers to the division of a segment into two parts, such that the whole segment is to the larger part as the larger part is to the smaller. What is the ratio of the smaller part to the larger in this case?

b) Let $a$ be the base of an isosceles triangle with a base angle of $72^{\circ}$, and $b$ be its lateral side. Prove that the segments $a$ and $b$ divide the segment $a+b$ in the golden section.
solution:
1.11. a) Answer: $\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$. Let the segment be divided into two segments of lengths $y$ and $z$, where $y<z$. We have the golden section if and only if $\frac{y}{z}=\frac{z}{y+z}=x$, where $x$ is the number we are looking for. For $x$, we get the equation $x(x+1)=\frac{y}{z} \frac{y+z}{z}=1$. Solving it and discarding the negative root, we get $x=-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$.

b) Let $ABC$ be a triangle with angles $\angle A=36^{\circ}, \angle B=\angle C=72^{\circ}$. Let, further, $a=BC$ and $b=AC$. Draw the angle bisector $BK$ in this triangle. Then $\angle KBC=36^{\circ}$, so triangle $BCK$ is also isosceles with the base angle $72^{\circ}$. Moreover, $AK=KB$, since $\angle ABK=36^{\circ}=\angle BAK$. Therefore, $KC=b-a$, so the equality $\frac{AB}{BC}=\frac{BC}{KC}$ is written as $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{a}{b-a}$, i.e., $b^{2}-ba=a^{2}$. Consequently, $\frac{a+b}{b}=\frac{b}{a}$, which is what we needed.

Method 2 Let $S=\{1,2, \cdots, 14\}, S^{\prime}=\{1,2, \cdots, 10\}$.

5. Given a function $f(x)$ defined on $\mathbb{R}$, for any $x \in \mathbb{R}$, we have
$$
\begin{array}{l}
f(-x)+f(x)=0 \\
f(x+1)+f(x)=0
\end{array}
$$

and when $x \in(0,1)$, $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$. Then, when $x \in\left[-3,-\frac{5}{2}\right]$, the range of $f(x)$ is
solution:
Solution: $\left(-1,-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right] \cup\{0\}$.
$f(x)$ is an odd function on $\mathbb{R}$, and from $f(x+1)+f(x)=0$, we have $f(x+2)=-f(x+1)=f(x)$. Thus, $f(x)$ has a period of 2.
Therefore, $f(1)=f(-1+2)=f(-1)=-f(1)$, so $f(1)=0$.
Thus, $f(-3)=f(-3+4)=f(1)=0$.
When $x \in\left[-3,-\frac{5}{2}\right]$, $x+2 \in\left[-1,-\frac{1}{2}\right]$, and $-x-2 \in\left[\frac{1}{2}, 1\right]$.
Hence, $f(x)=f(x+2)=-f(-x-2)=-\sqrt{-x-2}$.
Therefore, when $x \in\left[-3,-\frac{5}{2}\right]$, the range of $f(x)$ is $\left(-1,-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right] \cup\{0\}$.

problem: 37. Can we find a point in this convex polygon such that all projections of it onto the lines containing the sides of the polygon fall not on the sides themselves, but only on their extensions?
solution:
37. Such a point does not exist. To prove this, consider an arbitrary point \( P \) belonging to the convex polygon \( A_{1} A_{2} \ldots A_{n} \). Among the lines containing the sides of the polygon, choose the one closest to point \( P \) - let this be the line \( A_{2} A_{3} \). If we assume that the projection of point \( P \) onto \( (A_{2} A_{3}) \) does not belong to \( [A_{2} A_{3}] \), but, for example, lies on \( [A_{2} A_{3}) \), then it is obvious that the distance from point \( M \) to the next line \( A_{3} A_{4} \) is less than the distance from \( P \) to \( (A_{2} A_{3}) \), which contradicts the choice of \( (A_{2} A_{3}) \).

This problem has the following mechanical interpretation. Imagine that a light cardboard box is glued with a base in the shape of the given polygon (Fig. 57) and a weight, whose mass significantly exceeds the mass of the box, is attached at point \( P \). By placing such a box on its side on a horizontal plane, we see that if the projection \( P' \) of point \( P \) onto \( (AB) \) falls on the extension of segment \( AB \), then the force of gravity of the weight will cause the box to rotate and stand on side \( [BC] \). If the projection of point \( P \) also falls on the extension of \( [BC] \), the box will rotate again and stand on the next side, and so on. Therefore, if the projections of the weight always fell on the extensions of the sides in the same direction, the movement would continue indefinitely. Since such self-moving boxes do not exist, a point with the property indicated in the problem does not exist!

problem:
4. We call a set of professors and committees on which they serve a university if
(1) given two distinct professors there is one and only one committee on which they both serve,
(2) given any committee, $C$, and any professor, $P$, not on that committee, there is exactly one committee on which $P$ serves and no professors on committee $C$ serve, and
(3) there are at least two professors on each committee; there are at least two committees.
What is the smallest number of committees a university can have?
solution:
Solution: Let $C$ be any committee. Then there exists a professor $P$ not on $C$ (or else there would be no other committees). By axiom 2, $P$ serves on a committee $D$ having no common members with $C$. Each of these committees has at least two members, and for each $Q \in C, R \in D$, there exists (by axiom 1) a committee containing $Q$ and $R$, which (again by axiom 1) has no other common members with $C$ or $D$. Thus we have at least
$2+2 \cdot 2=6$ committees. This minimum is attainable - just take four professors and let any two professors form a committee.

problem: 4.1. A train of length $L=600$ m, moving by inertia, enters a hill with an angle of inclination $\alpha=30^{\circ}$ and stops when exactly a quarter of the train is on the hill. What was the initial speed of the train $V$ (in km/h)? Provide the nearest whole number to the calculated speed. Neglect friction and assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g=10 \mathrm{m} /$ sec $^{2}$.
solution:
Answer: 49. Solution. The kinetic energy of the train $\frac{m v^{2}}{2}$ will be equal to the potential energy of the part of the train that has entered the hill $\frac{1}{2} \frac{L}{4} \sin \alpha \frac{m}{4} g$.

Then we get $V^{2}=\frac{L}{4} \frac{1}{8} *(3.6)^{2}=\frac{6000 *(3.6)^{2}}{32}=9 \sqrt{30}$.

Since the following double inequality is true $49<9 \sqrt{30}<49.5$ (verified by squaring), the answer is 49.

problem:
Anička and Maruška each have their favorite natural number. If we multiply Anička's number by itself, we get a number that is a hundred times larger than when we multiply Maruška's number by itself. If we add Anička's and Maruška's favorite numbers, we get a number that is 18 more than half of Anička's number.

Determine Anička's and Maruška's favorite numbers.

(E. Semerádová)

Hint. How many times is Anička's number larger than Maruška's?
solution:
Aniččino číslo is ten times larger than Maruščino číslo - only in this case is the product of Aniččino číslo with itself equal to the hundredfold of Maruščino číslo $(10 \cdot 10=100)$. Half of Aniččino číslo is therefore five times larger than Maruščino číslo.

The sum of Aniččino číslo and Maruščino číslo is 18 greater than half of Aniččino číslo. Therefore, 18 is the sum of half of Aniččino číslo and Maruščino číslo. According to the conclusion of the previous paragraph, this sum is equal to six times Maruščino číslo.

Thus, Maruščino číslo is $3(18: 6=3)$ and Aniččino číslo is $30(10 \cdot 3=30)$.

Note. If we denote Aniččino číslo by $a$ and Maruščino číslo by $m$, then the previous considerations can be summarized as follows:

- $a \cdot a=100 \mathrm{~m} \cdot \mathrm{m}$, so $a=10 \mathrm{~m}$, so $\frac{1}{2} a=5 \mathrm{~m}$.
- $a+m=\frac{1}{2} a+18$, so $18=\frac{1}{2} a+m=6 m$.
- $m=18: 6=3$ and $a=10 m=30$.

After the initial observation $(a=10 m)$, it is also possible to successively substitute natural numbers for $m$, express the relevant difference $\left(a+m-\frac{1}{2} a=\frac{1}{2} a+m\right)$, and check whether it is or is not equal to 18:

| $m$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | $\ldots$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| $a$ | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | $\ldots$ |
| $\frac{1}{2} a+m$ | 6 | 12 | 18 | 24 | $\ldots$ |

problem: 6. In her fourth year at Hogwarts, Hermione was outraged by the infringement of house-elf rights and founded the Association for the Restoration of Elven Independence. Of course, even the brightest and noblest idea requires funding for promotion, so Hermione decided to finance her campaign by producing merchandise, starting with the production of badges. Everyone at Hogwarts liked this idea, and Hermione secured the right to produce such badges by obtaining the relevant patent. Ron, who has known the nuances of magical technologies since childhood, convinced Hermione that the cost of producing badges would be $T C(Q)=5 Q^{2}$, where $Q$ is the number of badges produced. Harry, with the help of his friends and the time-turner potion, found out that the demand for badges from students of all houses except Slytherin can be represented by the demand function $q_{w s}=26-2 P$, and from Slytherin by the demand function $q_{s}=10-P$ (Slytherin students are prejudiced against ideas from Gryffindors, especially those of Muggle descent, but would not refuse to support the Association). What is the maximum amount Hermione can earn for her company by selling badges if the prices of the same product for different Hogwarts houses must be the same?
solution:
# Solution:

Since the prices must be the same for the faculties, Hermione Monopolist must take into account the aggregate demand for badges, which is given by:

$$
Q(P)=q_{w s}+q_{s}=\left\{\begin{array}{l}
26-2 P, P \geq 13 \\
36-3 P, P<13
\end{array}\right.
$$

Then the marginal revenue of Hermione's monopoly is given by:

$$
M R(Q)=(P(Q) Q)^{\prime}=\left\{\begin{array}{c}
13-Q, Q \leq 6 \\
12-2 Q / 3, Q>6
\end{array}\right.
$$

Since the marginal revenue of Hermione's monopoly is decreasing, and the marginal costs are increasing, the maximum profit of Hermione's enterprise will be achieved when $M R\left(Q^{*}\right)=M C\left(Q^{*}\right)$. Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M R\left(Q^{*}\right)=M C\left(Q^{*}\right) \\
& \rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}
13-Q=10 Q, \quad Q=13 / 11 \leq 6 \\
12-\frac{2 Q}{3}=10 Q, \quad Q=\frac{9}{8}, \text { which does not satisfy the condition } Q>6
\end{array}\right.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, only students from all faculties except Slytherin will buy the product.

In this case, $\frac{13}{11}$ units of the product will be sold at a price of $P=13-\frac{13}{22}=\frac{273}{22}$

It should be noted that the problem does not specify the units in which the quantity of badges is measured (for example, it could be pairs, tens, dozens, etc.).

Then the Association will earn $\frac{13}{11} * \frac{273}{22}-5 *\left(\frac{13}{11}\right)^{2} \approx 7.682$

problem: 5. A natural number, if the sum of its digits equals the product of its digits, is called a "coincidence number". Among five-digit numbers, there are $\qquad$ "coincidence numbers".

## Task 13/80

From an arbitrarily chosen natural number $n_{1}$, form a natural number $n_{2}$ by appending a three-digit natural number. For which numbers $\mathrm{n}$ is the sum $s=n_{1}+n_{2}$ divisible by 77 without a remainder?
solution:
It is $n_{2}=1000 n_{1}+n$, thus $s=n_{1}+n_{2}=1001 n_{1}+n$. Since $1001=7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13$ is divisible by $77=7 \cdot 11$, the divisibility of $s$ is determined precisely when $n$ is divisible by 77.

This yields the following 11 three-digit numbers $\mathrm{n}$:

$$
154 ; 231 ; 308 ; 385 ; 462 ; 539 ; 616 ; 693 ; 770 ; 847 ; 924
$$

If "improperly three-digit" numbers are also allowed, then 077 also satisfies the condition; if the number zero is included in the set of natural numbers, then $n=000$ must also be considered, so that a maximum of 13 numbers $n$ can be listed.

problem: 1. On an island, there live only knights, who always tell the truth, and liars, who always lie. One fine day, 30 islanders sat around a round table. Each of them can see everyone except themselves and their neighbors. Each person in turn said the phrase: "All I see are liars." How many liars were sitting at the table?
solution:
Answer: 28.

Solution. Not all of those sitting at the table are liars (otherwise they would all be telling the truth). Therefore, there is at least one knight sitting at the table. Everyone he sees is a liar. Let's determine who his neighbors are. Both of them cannot be liars (otherwise they would be telling the truth). Also, both of them cannot be knights, since they see each other. Therefore, one of them is a knight, and the other is a liar. It remains to note that the situation where two knights sit next to each other, and all the others are liars, is possible.

problem: 3. The height of an isosceles trapezoid is equal to $h$, and its area is equal to $h^{2}$. Determine the angle between the diagonals of this trapezoid.
solution:
Solution. Let $ABCD$ be an isosceles trapezoid ($AD = BC$), $CE$ be the perpendicular dropped from $C$ to the base $AB$, i.e., $CE = h$ (draw a diagram). From the condition of the problem, we have $\frac{a+b}{2} h = h^2$, from which we get $\frac{a+b}{2} = h$, which is the midline of the trapezoid. Then

$$
AE = AB - BE = a - \frac{a-b}{2} = \frac{a+b}{2} = h
$$

so $\measuredangle EAC = \measuredangle ABD = 45^{\circ}$. The angle between the diagonals, as the third angle of $\triangle ABO$, where $O$ is the intersection of the diagonals, is equal to $90^{\circ}$, which means that the diagonals intersect at a right angle.

solution:
B3. We multiply the equality by $\left(1+a^{2}\right)\left(1+b^{2}\right) \neq 0$ and simplify to obtain the equivalent equality $a^{2} b^{2}=1$. Therefore, $a b= \pm 1$. We also simplify the given expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(a+b)\left(\frac{a}{1+a^{2}}+\frac{b}{1+b^{2}}\right) & =(a+b) \frac{a+a b^{2}+b+a^{2} b}{\left(1+a^{2}\right)\left(1+b^{2}\right)}=(a+b) \frac{(a+b)(1+a b)}{\left(1+a^{2}\right)\left(1+b^{2}\right)}= \\
& =\frac{\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+2 a b\right)(1+a b)}{1+a^{2}+b^{2}+a^{2} b^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

If $a b=-1$, the value of this expression is 0. If $a b=1$, the value of this expression is

$$
\frac{\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+2\right) \cdot 2}{a^{2}+b^{2}+2}=2
$$

We can verify that these two values are indeed achievable. The value 0 is achieved, for example, when $a=1$ and $b=-1$, and the value 2 when $a=b=1$.

problem:
1A. In the set of real numbers, solve the equation

$$
\frac{1}{x^{2}}+\frac{1}{(\sqrt{5}-x)^{2}}=7
$$
solution:
Solution. Clearly, $x \notin\{0, \sqrt{5}\}$. We introduce the substitution $y=\sqrt{5}-x$ and obtain the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x+y=\sqrt{5} \\
\frac{1}{x^{2}}+\frac{1}{y^{2}}=7
\end{array}\right.
$$

We have,

$$
7=\frac{1}{x^{2}}+\frac{1}{y^{2}}=\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{x^{2} y^{2}}=\frac{(x+y)^{2}-2 x y}{(x y)^{2}}=\frac{5-2 x y}{(x y)^{2}}
$$

hence $7(x y)^{2}+2 x y-5=0$, from which we get $x y=\frac{5}{7}$ or $x y=-1$. From $x+y=\sqrt{5}$ and $x y=\frac{5}{7}$, it follows that $x$ and $y$ are solutions to the quadratic equation $z^{2}-z \sqrt{5}+\frac{5}{7}=0$, that is, $x, y=\frac{7 \sqrt{5} \pm \sqrt{105}}{14}$. From $x+y=\sqrt{5}$, we get $x=\sqrt{5}-y=\sqrt{5}-\frac{7 \sqrt{5} \pm \sqrt{105}}{14}=\frac{7 \sqrt{5} \mp \sqrt{105}}{14}$, so the equation in $x$ has the solutions $x_{1,2}=\frac{7 \sqrt{5} \pm \sqrt{105}}{14}$. From $x+y=\sqrt{5}$ and $x y=-1$, it follows that $x$ and $y$ are solutions to the quadratic equation $z^{2}-z \sqrt{5}+-1=0$, that is, $x, y=\frac{\sqrt{5} \pm 3}{2}$. From $x+y=\sqrt{5}$, we get $x=\sqrt{5}-y=\sqrt{5}-\frac{\sqrt{5} \pm 3}{2}=\frac{\sqrt{5} \mp 3}{2}$, so the equation in $x$ has the solutions $x_{3,4}=\frac{\sqrt{5} \pm 3}{2}$.

solution:

In one cubic meter of air, there is $400 \cdot 5 \cdot 10^{-6}=0.002$ kg of water.

problem: 7. (4 points) Find what $x+y$ can be equal to, given that $x^{3}+6 x^{2}+16 x=-15$ and $y^{3}+6 y^{2}+16 y=-17$.
solution:
Answer: -4

Solution: Let $u=x+2$ and $v=y+2$. Then the original equations transform into $u^{3}+4 u=1$ and $v^{3}+4 v=-1$. Adding these equations, we get $(u+v)\left(u^{2}-u v+v^{2}+4\right)=0$. The second bracket is always positive, so the first one must be zero, from which we have $x+y=u+v-4=-4$.

Solve the following equation:

$$
\sqrt{x+1999 \sqrt{x+1999 \sqrt{x+1999 \sqrt{x+1999 \sqrt{2000 x}}}}}=x
$$
solution:
It is easily visible that 0 and 2000 are solutions to the equation. We will show that there are no other solutions.

Indeed, if $0\sqrt{x^{2}}=x$ then

$$
\sqrt{x+1999 \sqrt{2000 x}}>\sqrt{x+1999 x}=\sqrt{2000 x}>x
$$

and so on, the quantity under each square root on the left side of the equation is greater than $x$. Thus, the left side of the equation is greater than $x$, while the right side is equal to $x$, which is not possible.

If $x>2000$, then after $\sqrt{2000 x}<\sqrt{x^{2}}=x$, a similar reasoning shows that the left side of the equation is less than $x$, so we do not get a solution in this case either.

Remark. Taraza Busra (Budapest, ELTE Apáczai Cs. J. Gyak. Gimn., 12. o.t.) essentially followed the previous line of thought and generally proved that the

$$
\sqrt{\underbrace{x+n \sqrt{\cdots+n \sqrt{x+n \sqrt{(n+1) x}}}}_{k \text { terms }}}=x
$$

equation (where $n$ and $k$ are positive integers) has exactly two solutions, $x=0$ and $x=n+1$.

solution:
(a) (i) The semi-circles with diameter $Y Z, X Z$ and $X Y$ have diameters of length $x, y$ and $z$, and so have radii of length $\frac{1}{2} x, \frac{1}{2} y$ and $\frac{1}{2} z$, respectively.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_04_30_1271530ef38a72b7fb44g-06.jpg?height=377&width=426&top_left_y=278&top_left_x=988)

In terms of $x$, the area of a semi-circle with radius $\frac{1}{2} x$ is $\frac{1}{2} \pi\left(\frac{1}{2} x\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{8} \pi x^{2}$. (This is one-half of the area of the circle with radius $\frac{1}{2} x$.)

Similarly, in terms of $y$ and $z$, the areas of the semi-circles with diameter $X Z$ and $X Y$ are $\frac{1}{8} \pi y^{2}$ and $\frac{1}{8} \pi z^{2}$, respectively.

Therefore, $\frac{1}{8} \pi x^{2}=50 \pi$ and $\frac{1}{8} \pi y^{2}=288 \pi$ and we want to determine $\frac{1}{8} \pi z^{2}$.

Since $\triangle X Y Z$ is right-angled at $Z$, then $Y Z^{2}+X Z^{2}=X Y^{2}$, by the Pythagorean Theorem, and so $x^{2}+y^{2}=z^{2}$.

Multiplying both sides of this equation by $\frac{1}{8} \pi$, we obtain $\frac{1}{8} \pi x^{2}+\frac{1}{8} \pi y^{2}=\frac{1}{8} \pi z^{2}$.

Therefore, $50 \pi+288 \pi=\frac{1}{8} \pi z^{2}$ and so $\frac{1}{8} \pi z^{2}=338 \pi$.

Thus, the area of the semi-circle with diameter $X Y$ is $\frac{1}{8} \pi z^{2}=338 \pi$.

(Note that we did not need to determine $x, y$ or $z$.)

Multiplying both sides of this equation by 2 , we obtain $2 p^{2}+2 q^{2}=2 r^{2}$, and so $(\sqrt{2} p)^{2}+(\sqrt{2} q)^{2}=(\sqrt{2} r)^{2}$ or $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$.

Thus, the lengths $a, b$ and $c$ satisfy the Pythagorean equation, which tells us that the triangle formed with side lengths $a, b$ and $c$ is a right-angled triangle.

Note that the Pythagorean Theorem has two parts:

Suppose that $\triangle X Y Z$ has side lengths $Y Z=x, X Z=y$ and $X Y=z$. Then:

problem: 4. Calculate: $\log _{2} \prod_{a=0}^{20182} \prod_{b=0}^{2018}\left(1+\mathrm{e}^{\frac{2 a b k i}{2019}}\right)$.
solution:
4. 6725.

Notice,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\log _{2} \prod_{a=0}^{20182} \prod_{b=0}^{2018}\left(1+\mathrm{e}^{\frac{2 a b \pi j}{2019}}\right) \\
=\log _{2} \prod_{a=1}^{20192} \prod_{b=1}^{2019}\left(1+\mathrm{e}^{\frac{2 a b k x_{j}}{2019}}\right) .
\end{array}
$$

Generalize 2019 to a positive odd number $n$.
Let $(a, n)=d$. Then
$$
a=d a_{1}, n=d n_{1} \text {, and }\left(a_{1}, n_{1}\right)=1 ; a_{1}, 2 a_{1} \text {, }
$$
$\cdots, n_{1} a_{1}$ are a permutation of $1,2, \cdots, n_{1}$ modulo $n_{1}$.

Let $\omega=\mathrm{e}^{\frac{2 x_{1}}{1_{1}}}$, then $\omega^{a_{1}}, \omega^{2 a_{1}}, \cdots, \omega^{n_{1} a_{1}}$ are a permutation of $\omega, \omega^{2}$, $\cdots, \omega^{n_{1}}$.
Lemma If $n$ is a positive odd number, then
$$
\prod_{b=1}^{n}\left(1+\mathrm{e}^{\frac{2 a n k}{n}}\right)=2^{d}(d=(a, n)) \text {. }
$$

Proof Notice,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\prod_{b=1}^{n_{1}}\left(1+\mathrm{e}^{\frac{2 a n k i}{n}}\right)=\prod_{b=1}^{n_{1}}\left(1+\mathrm{e}^{\frac{2 a_{1} \omega_{n} i}{n_{1}}}\right) \\
=\prod_{b=1}^{n_{1}}\left(1+\omega^{b}\right),
\end{array}

problem: 2. Determine for which natural numbers $n$ it is possible to fill an $n \times n$ table with numbers $2a-1$ in such a way that the sum of all numbers in each row and each column is equal to 0. (Ján Mazák)
solution:
SOLUTION. Let us choose any row (or column) of the $n \times n$ square table, which is filled with numbers $2 \mathrm{a}-1$. Let $d$ be the number of 2s and $p$ be the number of -1s in it. Then $d+p=n$ and according to the problem statement, it must also hold that $2 d-p=0$. By adding these two equations, we get $3 d=n$, which means that the number $n$ must be divisible by three, i.e., $n=3 k$, where $k$ is a natural number.

We will show that this condition is also sufficient. For any $n=3 k$, we can divide the $n \times n$ table in an obvious way into $k^{2}$ smaller $3 \times 3$ square tables. It is easy to see that each of these smaller $3 \times 3$ tables can be filled in the required way - for example, by writing the number 2 in all three fields of one of its diagonals and the number -1 in the six remaining fields of this table. The entire $n \times n$ square table then satisfies the condition of the problem because each of the $k^{2}$ created $3 \times 3$ tables satisfies it.

Conclusion. The given method can fill exactly those $n \times n$ tables where $n$ is a natural number divisible by three.

## GUIDING AND ADDITIONAL PROBLEMS:

N1. Decide whether a $3 \times 3$ square table can be filled with natural numbers from 1 to 9 such that each number is used exactly once and the sum of all numbers in each row and each column is divisible by a) two, b) three. [a) No — if the sum of the numbers in each row of the table were divisible by two, the sum of all numbers in the table would also be divisible by two. However, their sum is 45. b) Yes — it is easy to find a specific example.]

N2. Decide for which natural numbers $n$ a $n \times n$ square table can be filled with the numbers 1 and -1 such that the sum of all numbers in each row and each column is equal to 0. [For every even number $n$, the table $n \times n$ can be filled as required in the pattern of a black and white chessboard. For odd $n$, this is not possible, because in no row (column) can there be the same number of -1s and 1s.]

N3. Decide whether a $3 \times 3$ square table can be filled with natural numbers from 1 to 9 such that each number is used exactly once and the sum of all numbers in each row, each column, and both diagonals is the same (we get a so-called magic square). [Since the sum of the given nine numbers is 45, the sum of all numbers in each row and each column must be $45: 3=15$, which is an odd number. There is one more odd number than even numbers in the table. Additionally, $1+9=2+8=3+7=4+6=10$. Therefore, if the number 5 is in the middle of the table, it is easy to find a specific example of a possible way to fill this table.]

D1. A $3 \times 3$ table is filled with different natural numbers such that in each row and column, the sum of the extreme numbers is equal to the number written between them. Determine the smallest number that can be written in the middle of the table. [69-C-S-2]

D2. In how many ways can the numbers $\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ be written into the fields of a $2 \times 3$ table such that each is used exactly once and the sum of all numbers in each row and each column is divisible by three? [Math Kangaroo 2018, Junior category, problem 21 (48 possibilities).]

problem:
Task 1. For a positive integer $n$ that is not a power of two, we define $t(n)$ as the largest odd divisor of $n$ and $r(n)$ as the smallest positive odd divisor of $n$ that is not equal to 1. Determine all positive integers $n$ that are not powers of two and for which

$$
n=3 t(n)+5 r(n)
$$
solution:
Solution I. If $n$ is odd, then $t(n)=n$, so $3 t(n)$ is greater than $n$, contradiction. If $n$ is divisible by 2 but not by 4, then $t(n)=\frac{1}{2} n$ and $3 t(n)$ is again greater than $n$, contradiction again. We can conclude that $n$ must be divisible by 4 at least. If $n$ is divisible by 16, then $t(n) \leq \frac{1}{16} n$. Furthermore, $r(n) \leq t(n)$, so $3 t(n)+5 r(n) \leq 8 t(n) \leq \frac{1}{2} n < n$, contradiction. Therefore, $n$ is not divisible by 16. We can thus write $n=4 m$ or $n=8 m$ with $m \geq 3$ odd.

Suppose $n=4 m$ with $m \geq 3$ odd. Then $t(n)=m$, so $4 m=3 m+5 r(n)$, hence $5 r(n)=m$. Since $r(n)$ is equal to the smallest odd prime divisor of $n$, which is also the smallest prime divisor of $m$, $m$ must be of the form $m=5 p$ with $p \leq 5$ an odd prime number. Thus, $m=15$ or $m=25$, which gives $n=60$ or $n=100$. Both solutions are valid.

Suppose that $n=8 m$ with $m \geq 3$ odd. Again, $t(n)=m$, so $8 m=3 m+5 r(n)$, hence $5 r(n)=5 m$, or $r(n)=m$. We see that $m$ is prime. So $n=8 p$ with $p$ an odd prime number. This family of solutions is also valid.

We find the solutions to be $n=60, n=100$ and $n=8 p$ with $p$ an odd prime number.

problem: 7. Let positive real numbers $x, y$ satisfy $x^{2}+y^{2}+\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}=\frac{27}{4}$. Then the minimum value of $P=\frac{15}{x}-\frac{3}{4 y}$ is
solution:
7. 6 .

By the AM-GM inequality for three terms, we have
$$
\begin{array}{l}
x^{2}+\frac{1}{x}=\left(x^{2}+\frac{8}{x}+\frac{8}{x}\right)-\frac{15}{x} \geqslant 12-\frac{15}{x}, \\
y^{2}+\frac{1}{y}=\left(y^{2}+\frac{1}{8 y}+\frac{1}{8 y}\right)+\frac{3}{4 y} \geqslant \frac{3}{4}+\frac{3}{4 y} .
\end{array}
$$

Adding the two inequalities, we get
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\frac{27}{4}=x^{2}+y^{2}+\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y} \geqslant \frac{51}{4}+\left(\frac{3}{4 y}-\frac{15}{x}\right) \\
\Rightarrow P=\frac{15}{x}-\frac{3}{4 y} \geqslant 6 .
\end{array}
$$

Equality holds if and only if $x=2, y=\frac{1}{2}$. Therefore, the minimum value of $P$ is 6.

problem:
(Exercise 3.9 from the course notes)

Find the inverse of 37 modulo 53

Proposition 11 (Inverse of a product).

Proposition 12 (Proper inverse).
solution:
Sometimes, trial and error is enough, but here we proceed with certainty. We start by performing the Euclidean algorithm

\[
\begin{aligned}
& 53=37+16 \\
& 37=16 * 2+5 \\
& 16=5 * 3+1
\end{aligned}
\]

From this, we deduce a Bézout's identity

\[
\begin{array}{r}
16-5 * 3=1 \\
16-(37-16 * 2) * 3=1 \\
53-37-(37-(53-37) * 2) * 3=1 \\
7 * 53-10 * 37=1
\end{array}
\]

We look modulo 53: 10 is the inverse of 37 modulo 53.

problem:
3.1 Two ants are running along a circle towards each other at constant speeds. While one of them runs 9 laps, the other runs 6. At the point where the ants meet, a red dot appears. How many red dots will there be on the circle?

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_6a9b962ccc5e03d35f9eg-05.jpg?height=449&width=531&top_left_y=495&top_left_x=822)

#
solution:
# Answer: 5

Solution. The ratio of the speeds of the ants is $\frac{9}{6}=\frac{3}{2}$. Without loss of generality, assume the circumference of the circle is 5, and let the ants meet at some moment at point 0. Place points $1, 2, 3,$ and 4 clockwise so that they, together with point 0, divide the circle into 5 equal parts. If the slower ant runs counterclockwise, they will meet again at point 2. Now we can consider this point as the starting point, and thus they will meet next at point 4, and then at point 1 (since $4+2=6$, but the circumference is 5). The next meeting will be at point 3, then 0, after which the process will repeat, and there will be a total of 5 points.

problem:
Florinda went for a walk. She left point $A$ and walked $1 \mathrm{~m}$. At this point, she turned left at an angle of $90^{\circ}$ and walked $2 \mathrm{~m}$. At the last point, she turned left again and walked $3 \mathrm{~m}$. She continued walking in this manner until, on the last segment, she walked $30 \mathrm{~m}$ and reached her final point, which we will call point $B$. The following figure illustrates the first seven segments of Florinda's walk (note that point $B$ is not illustrated).

Calculate the distance between points $A$ and $B$.

#
solution:
Solution

In this exercise, all distances are given in meters. Observe in the following figure that the horizontal straight-line segments have odd lengths while the vertical ones have even lengths.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_01_463eeeabc25d438954b1g-43.jpg?height=354&width=355&top_left_y=526&top_left_x=732)

If we consider only the horizontal straight-line segments, we obtain that the total horizontal displacement is equal to

$$
1-3+5-7+9-11+13-\cdots+25-27+29
$$

To calculate this value, we can group the terms as follows:

$$
1 \underbrace{-3+5}_{+2} \underbrace{-7+9}_{+2} \underbrace{-11+13}_{+2}-\ldots \underbrace{-27+29}_{+2}
$$

The total horizontal displacement is, then, equal to $1+2 \times 7=15$.

Now considering the vertical displacements and calculating similarly, we obtain

$$
2 \underbrace{-4+6}_{+2} \underbrace{-8+10}_{+2} \underbrace{-12+14}_{+2}-\ldots \underbrace{-28+30}_{+2}=2+2 \times 7=16

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_01_463eeeabc25d438954b1g-43.jpg?height=460&width=471&top_left_y=1821&top_left_x=671)

Finally, by the Pythagorean Theorem, we conclude that the total displacement is equal to

$$
\sqrt{15^{2}+16^{2}}=\sqrt{481}
$$

problem:
Tolpygo A.K.

Two players are involved. The first player has 1000 even cards (2, 4, ..., 2000), and the second player has 1001 odd cards (1, 3, ..., 2001). They take turns, with the first player starting. A move consists of the following: the player whose turn it is lays down one of their cards, and the other player, after looking at it, lays down one of their cards; the player with the higher number on their card scores one point, and both laid-down cards are discarded. In total, there are 1000 moves (one card of the second player is not used). What is the maximum number of points each player can guarantee for themselves (regardless of how their opponent plays)?
solution:
Let's call a move critical if the card 2001 is used. We will prove that the first player can score points on all of the second player's moves, except, perhaps, the critical one.

At any moment, we will denote the first player's cards as $a_{1}b_{k}$. We will prove that the first player can maintain this situation until the critical move.

Specifically, on their turn, the first player plays with $a_{1}$, and they are left with the cards $A_{k}=a_{k+1}$ ( $k=1,2, \ldots, n-1$ ); for any response, the remaining cards of the second player satisfy $B_{k} \leq b_{k+1}b_{k+1}$. Similarly, we verify that the first player can maintain this situation until the end of the game: on their turn, they give up $a_{1}$, and on the second player's turn, they place $a_{k}$ on $b_{k+1}$ (and $a_{1}$ on $\left.b_{1}\right)$.

Now, let's prove that the second player can score points on all of the first player's moves plus on their last move. In the same notation, at the beginning, the inequalities $b_{k+1}>a_{k}$ are satisfied. Acting according to the strategy outlined above (on their turn - place $b_{1}$, on the first player's turn - place $b_{k+1}$ on $a_{k}$), the second player maintains this situation and scores points on all of the first player's moves. Before the last move, the second player is left with the largest card at that moment, $b_{2}$.

By placing it, they score an additional point.

## Answer

First player - 499 points, second player - 501.

This second method for determining the coefficients of the power series that satisfies the given differential equation, which is based on the use of the Maclaurin series*, in some cases requires less computational work than the method of undetermined coefficients. It is applicable for finding the general or particular integrals of the equation if it is solvable with respect to the highest-order derivative and if it is possible to obtain a derivative of any order by its successive differentiation.

Integration of equations using series is of great importance, however, it should be noted that not every equation can yield an integral in the form of a suitable power series.

For example, the equation $x^{2} y^{\prime}-y(x+1)=-x^{2}$ (linear) has the general integral

$$
y=\frac{x}{\sqrt[x]{e}}\left(c-\int \frac{\sqrt[x]{e}}{x} d x\right)
$$

However, assuming that there exists an integral in the form of a power series (1) and determining its coefficients, we obtain the series

$$
y=x^{2}\left(1+1!x+2!x^{2}+3!x^{3}+\ldots+n!x^{4}+\ldots\right)
$$

which is practically unusable, as it diverges for any value of $x$ different from zero.

problem:
[ Projections of the bases, sides, or vertices of a trapezoid ]  [ Properties and characteristics of an isosceles triangle. ]

In a right trapezoid, the smaller diagonal is equal to the larger lateral side.

Find the larger diagonal if the larger lateral side is equal to $a$, and the smaller base is equal to $b$.
solution:
Prove that the larger base is twice as large as the smaller one.

## Solution

Let $CD$ be the larger lateral side of trapezoid $ABCD$, $BC$ be the smaller base, $CD=a$, $BC=b$, and $BD$ be the larger diagonal. Drop a perpendicular $CM$ to the larger base $AD$. Since $AC=CD$, then $AM=MD$, and since $AM=BC=b$, then $AD=2b$. Therefore, $AB^2=CM^2=a^2-b^2$. Consequently, $BD^2=AB^2+AD^2=4b^2+a^2-b^2=a^2+3b^2$.

## Answer

$\sqrt{a^2+3b^2}$.

Let's rotate each edge of a regular tetrahedron by \(180^{\circ}\) around the opposite edge. What shape is defined by the six resulting lines?
solution:
It is known that four appropriate vertices of a cube and the six face diagonals determined by them (Fig. 1) precisely give the vertices and edges of a regular tetrahedron. Let's take a large cube made up of 27 identical small cubes and place the vertices of a regular tetrahedron at the center of the small cube (Fig. 2), labeling the vertices as shown in the figure.

Rotate the $E G F H$ face around $A C$ by $180^{\circ}$. The rotated plane $E F G H$ will be parallel to the plane $E F G H$, and it will be at the same distance from $A C$ as $E F G H$. There is only one such plane, the $I J K L$ plane, so the image of $E F G H$ is $I J K L$. Due to the properties of the cube, the line $F H$ lies in the perpendicular bisector plane of the segment $A C$. During the rotation, the image of this plane is itself, so the image of $F H$ also lies in the perpendicular bisector plane. This means that the image of $F H$ can only be the intersection of the perpendicular bisector plane and the $I J K L$ plane, which is the line $J L$.

Similarly, we can show that the image of each edge line of the small tetrahedron after rotation is a face diagonal of the large cube, and these six face diagonals are such that three of them meet at each vertex of the large cube. Thus, the six lines in the problem define a regular tetrahedron whose edge length is three times the edge length of the original tetrahedron.

problem:
For each of the following equations, determine the set of polynomials $P \in \mathbb{K}[X]$ satisfying the condition.

1. $P \circ P=P$
2. $P\left(X^{2}\right)=\left(X^{2}+1\right) P(X)$
3. $P(2 X)=P(X)-1$
4. $16 P\left(X^{2}\right)=P(2 X)^{2}$
solution:
At each step, proceed by analysis-synthesis considering the degree and leading coefficient. Also, always look for obvious solutions to guide the reasoning.

Finally, all classical methods of functional equations are of course relevant.

1. Constant polynomials are solutions.

If $P$ is a non-constant solution, then $\operatorname{deg}(P)^{2}=\operatorname{deg}(P)$, hence $\operatorname{deg}(P)=1$.

Moreover, $P=a X+b$ is a solution if and only if $a(a X+b)+b=a X+b c'$, which means $a^{2}=a$ and $a b+b=b$.

The solutions are therefore the constant polynomials and $X$.

2. If $P$ is a solution, then $2 \operatorname{deg}(P)=2+\operatorname{deg}(P)$, hence $\operatorname{deg}(P)=-\infty$ or $\operatorname{deg}(P)=2$.

We can then continue the analysis, for example by noting that $P(1)=2 P(1)$, hence $P(1)=0$ and $2 P(-1)=P(1)$, hence $P(-1)=0$, so $X^{2}-1 \mid P$, etc., or simply solve the $3 \times 3$ system without thinking.

A polynomial $P=a X^{2}+b X+c$ is a solution if and only if $a X^{4}+b X^{2}+c=a X^{4}+b X^{3}+(a+c) X^{2}+b X+c$ $c'$, which means

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
a & =a \\
b & =0 \\
a+c & =0 \\
b & =0 \\
c & =c
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

or equivalently $a=-c$ and $b=0$.

We thus obtain (after synthesis) that the solutions are the

$$
\lambda\left(X^{2}-1\right), \lambda \in \mathbb{K}
$$

3. No non-constant polynomial is a solution.

Moreover, if $P$ of degree $n \geqslant 1$ and leading coefficient $a_{n} \neq 0$ is a solution, then $2^{n} a_{n}=a_{n}$. Therefore, there is no solution.

4. The zero polynomial is a solution.

Moreover, if $P$ of degree $n \geqslant 0$ and leading coefficient $a_{n} \neq 0$ is a solution, then $16 a_{n}=\left(2^{n} a_{n}\right)^{2}$, hence $n=2$ and $a_{n}=1$.

With $P=a X^{2}+b X+c$, $P$ is a solution if and only if

$$
16 a X^{4}+16 b X^{2}+16 c=\left(4 a X^{2}+2 b X+c\right)^{2}
$$

which means, after expanding,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
16 a & =16 a^{2} \\
0 & =16 a b \\
16 b & =8 a c+4 b^{2} \\
0 & =4 b c \\
c & =c^{2}
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$c'$, which means $a=1, b=0, c=0$. Therefore (after synthesis) the only non-zero solution is $X^{2}$.

problem: 13.450 If at the beginning of the time measurement there were $m_{0}$ g of substance $A$ and $2 m_{0}$ g of substance $B$, then after any number $t$ years, as a result of the radioactive decay of these substances, there will remain respectively $\boldsymbol{m}=\boldsymbol{m}_{0} \cdot 2^{-\lambda_{1} t}$ and $M=2 m_{0} \cdot 2^{-\lambda_{2} t}$, where $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ are constants depending on the nature of the substances. Calculate the half-life of each of these substances, i.e., find out after how many years only half of the initial amount of each substance will remain, if it is known that the half-life of substance $B$ is two times less than that of substance $A$, and that after 20 years the total mass of these substances decreases by 8 times.
solution:
Solution. Let $x$ and $2x$ be the half-lives of the second and first substances, respectively. According to the conditions,

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
m_{0} \cdot 2^{-\lambda_{1} \cdot 2x} = \frac{m_{0}}{2}, \\
2m_{0} \cdot 2^{-\lambda_{2} \cdot x} = m_{0}, \\
m_{0} \cdot 2^{-\lambda_{1} \cdot 20} + 2m_{0} \cdot 2^{-\lambda_{2} \cdot 20} = \frac{3m_{0}}{8}
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
2^{-2\lambda_{1} x + 1} = 1 \\
2^{-\lambda_{2} \cdot x + 1} = 1 \\
8 \cdot 2^{-20\lambda_{1}} + 16 \cdot 2^{-20\lambda_{2}} = 3
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

From the first two equations, it follows that $\lambda_{1} = \frac{1}{2x}, \lambda_{2} = \frac{1}{x}$.

Substituting these values into the third equation, we get: $16 \cdot 2^{-\frac{20}{x}} + 8 \cdot 2^{-\frac{10}{x}} - 3 = 0$.

Let $y = 2^{-\frac{10}{x}}$, then we have:

$16y^{2} + 8y - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow y = 2^{-2} \Rightarrow 2^{-\frac{10}{x}} = 2^{-2} \Rightarrow x = 5$.

Answer: 10 years, 5 years.

problem: 1. Two players, A and B, play a game on a $6 \times 6$ grid. Each turn, a player writes a real number in an empty cell, ensuring that the number is different from all numbers already written in the grid. A starts, and then they take turns. Once every cell is filled, the cell containing the largest number in each row is colored black. A wins if they can draw a straight line from the top to the bottom of the grid such that every point on the line is within a black cell (including the boundaries of the black cells). Otherwise, B wins. Who has a winning strategy? ? ${ }^{[6]}$
solution:
【Analysis】Answer: 15.
If Player A keeps all the hearts, all the A, K, Q cards for himself, then Player B cannot score when Player A plays the Ace, King, and Queen of hearts. Player B cannot guarantee getting more than 15 points.

The following proof shows that no matter how Player A retains the cards for himself, Player B can ensure getting no less than 15 points.

Imagine placing all the cards in a 4x9 grid (cards in the same column have the same value, and cards in the same row have the same suit).

First, prove that if Player A marks 18 cards as black (the remaining 18 cards are white), then Player B can always separate at least 15 "good pairs": each pair consists of one black card and one white card, either in the same column or in the same row.

Thus, when Player A plays the black card in a pair, Player B can respond with the white card in the pair, thereby scoring.

Classify the columns based on the number of black cards in them. For example, if a column has 3 black cards, it is called a 3-type column.
(1) Player B first observes the 2-type columns. As long as there are such columns, each can be divided into two good pairs.
(2) Then observe the "column pairs" of 0-type and 4-type. Clearly, each such column pair can be divided into 4 good pairs.
(3) Then observe the column pairs of 1-type and 3-type. Each such column pair can similarly be divided into 4 good pairs (as shown in Figure 1, cells with the same number are paired).
(4) If there are no such column pairs, then by symmetry, it can be assumed that only 1-type and 4-type "single" columns remain. If there are \(a\) 4-type columns and \(b\) 1-type columns, then \(4a + b = 3b\), which means \(b = 2a\). In each "column group" consisting of one 4-type column and two 1-type columns, Player B can ensure at least 5 good pairs, as shown in Figure 2.

Since \(3a = a + b \leq 9\), there are at most 3 "bad pairs" left in the grid, meaning Player B can lose at most 3 points.
In summary, Player B can ensure getting at least 15 points.

problem: 51. In a box, there are 250 light bulbs, of which 100 are 100W, 50 are 60W, 50 are 25W, and 50 are 15W. Calculate the probability that the power of any randomly selected light bulb will not exceed 60W.
solution:
Solution. Let $A$ be the event that the power of the bulb is $60 \mathrm{Wt}$, $B$-- $25 \mathrm{Wt}$, $C$-- $15 \mathrm{Wt}$, $D$-- $100$ Wt. Events $A, B, C$ and $D$ form a complete system, as they are all mutually exclusive and one of them will definitely occur in the given trial (selection of a bulb). The probability of one of them occurring is a certain event, i.e., $P(A)+P(B)+P(C)+P(D)=1$.

Events "the power of the bulb is no more than 60 Wt" and "the power of the bulb is more than $60 \mathrm{Wt}$" are opposite. According to the property of opposite events, we have $P(A)+P(B)+P(C)=1-P(D)$. Considering that $P(A)+P(B)+P(C)=P(A+B+C)$, we get $P(A+B+C)=1-$ $-P(D)$, hence $P(A+B+C)=1-\frac{100}{250}$, i.e., $P(A+B+C)=\frac{3}{5}$.

problem:
\left.\begin{array}{l}{[\text { Product of the lengths of chord segments and secant segments ] }} \\ {[\quad \text { Diameter, main properties }}\end{array}\right]

Point $P$ is 7 units away from the center of a circle with a radius of 11. A chord passing through point $P$ is 18 units long. Find the segments into which the chord is divided by point $P$?
solution:
Drop a perpendicular from the center of the circle to the given chord.

## Solution

## First method.

Let $O$ be the center of the given circle, $AB$ be the given chord, $AB=18, OP=7$. Let $M$ be the foot of the perpendicular dropped from the center $O$ to the chord $AB$. Then $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$ and

$$
OM=\sqrt{OA^2-AM^2}=\sqrt{40}
$$

If point $P$ is between $M$ and $B$, then

$$
PM=\sqrt{OP^2-OM^2}=3
$$

Second method.

Let $O$ be the center of the circle, $AB$ be the given chord. Draw the diameter $CD$ passing through point $P$ ($P$ is between $O$ and $D$). Let $PB=x$. Then

$$
\begin{gathered}
AP=18-x, DP=OD-OP=11-7=4 \\
PC=OP+OC=7+11=18, AP \cdot PB=PD \cdot PC
\end{gathered}
$$

or

$$
(18-x) x=4 \cdot 18
$$

From this equation, we find that $x=12$ or $x=6$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_36c4956010bd91c4b4eeg-05.jpg?height=497&width=489&top_left_y=532&top_left_x=790)

Answer

12 and 6.

problem: 11. (20 points) Given the ellipse $\Gamma: \frac{x^{2}}{4}+y^{2}=1$, point $P(1,0)$, lines $l_{1}: x=-2, l_{2}: x=2$, $AB$ and $CD$ are two chords of the ellipse $\Gamma$ passing through point $P$, and the line $l_{CD}$: $x=1$, lines $AC$ and $BD$ intersect $l_{2}$ and $l_{1}$ at points $E$ and $F$ respectively. Find the ratio of the y-coordinates of points $E$ and $F$.
solution:
11. Let's assume point \( C\left(1, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right), D\left(1,-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \)
\[
\begin{array}{l}
l_{A B}: t y=x-1, A\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right), B\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right), \\
E(2, e), F(-2, f) .
\end{array}
\]

By combining the equation of line \( A B \) with the equation of the ellipse \( \Gamma \), we get
\[
\begin{array}{l}
(t y+1)^{2}+4 y^{2}-4=0 \\
\Rightarrow\left(t^{2}+4\right) y^{2}+2 t y-3=0 .
\end{array}
\]

By Vieta's formulas, we have
\[
y_{1}+y_{2}=\frac{-2 t}{t^{2}+4}, y_{1} y_{2}=\frac{-3}{t^{2}+4} \text {. }
\]

Since points \( A, C, E \) are collinear,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow & \frac{x_{1}-1}{2-1}=\frac{y_{1}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{e-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \\
\Rightarrow e & =\frac{y_{1}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{x_{1}-1}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\
& =\frac{y_{1}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{t y_{1}}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\
& =\frac{1}{t}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{t y_{1}}\right) .
\end{aligned}
\]

Since points \( B, D, F \) are collinear,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow & \frac{x_{2}-1}{-2-1}=\frac{y_{2}-\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{2}}{f-\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{2}} \\
\Rightarrow f & =\frac{-3\left(y_{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}{x_{2}-1}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\
& =\frac{-3\left(y_{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}{t y_{2}}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\
& =\frac{-3}{t}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\left(1+\frac{3}{t y_{2}}\right) .
\end{aligned}
\]

Then \( 3 e+f \)
\[
\begin{array}{l}
=3\left(\frac{1}{t}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot \frac{t y_{1}-1}{t y_{1}}\right)+\frac{-3}{t}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot \frac{t y_{2}+3}{t y_{2}} \\
=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\left(3-\frac{3}{t y_{1}}-1-\frac{3}{t y_{2}}\right) .
\end{array}
\]

Since \(\frac{1}{t y_{1}}+\frac{1}{t y_{2}}=\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}}{t y_{1} y_{2}}=\frac{\frac{-2 t}{t^{2}+4}}{t \cdot \frac{-3}{t^{2}+4}}=\frac{2}{3}\), we have
\[
3 e+f=0 \text {. }
\]

Therefore, the required value is \( -\frac{1}{3} \).

problem:
## Task B-2.6.

The equations $|z-2 a|=|z-a| \text{ and } |z-3 a i|=|z-a i|, a \in \mathbb{R}, a \neq 0, z \in \mathbb{C}$, determine sets of points in the Gaussian plane that, together with the coordinate axes, enclose a figure with an area of 75 square units. Calculate the perimeter of this figure.
solution:
## Solution.

If $z=x+y i, x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, the equation $|z-2 a|=|z-a|$ transforms into

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sqrt{(x-2 a)^{2}+y^{2}}=\sqrt{(x-a)^{2}+y^{2}} \\
& (x-2 a)^{2}+y^{2}=(x-a)^{2}+y^{2} \\
& x^{2}-4 a x+4 a^{2}=x^{2}-2 a x+a^{2} \\
& 2 a x=3 a^{2} \\
& x=\frac{3}{2} a
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first set of points is a line perpendicular to the $x$-axis, $x=\frac{3}{2} a$.

By an analogous procedure, the second equation $|z-3 a i|=|z-a i|$ transforms into

$$
\sqrt{x^{2}+(y-3 a)^{2}}=\sqrt{x^{2}+(y-a)^{2}}
$$

which, after simplification, gives $y=2 a$, a line perpendicular to the $y$-axis.

The obtained lines, together with the coordinate axes, form a rectangle with side lengths $\frac{3}{2}|a|$ and $2|a|$.

It follows that $P=\frac{3}{2} \cdot 2 a^{2}=75 \Rightarrow a=5$ or $a=-5$.

The perimeter of the obtained figure is $O=2 \cdot \frac{3}{2} a+2 \cdot 2 a=7 a=35$ units.

Note: If a student recognizes that the equations $|z-2 a|=|z-a|$ and $|z-3 a i|=|z-a i|$ represent the perpendicular bisectors of segments, this should be recognized and all the points for that part of the task should be awarded.

problem: 1. (5 points) Find the value of the function $f(x)$ at the point $x_{0}=1000$, if $f(0)=1$ and for any $x$ the equality $f(x+2)=f(x)+4 x+2$ holds.
solution:
Answer: 999001

Solution: In the equation $f(x+2)-f(x)=4 x+2$, we will substitute for $x$ the numbers $0,2,4, \ldots, 998$. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& f(2)-f(0)=4 \cdot 0+2 \\
& f(4)-f(2)=4 \cdot 2+2
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(1000)-f(998)=4 \cdot 998+2
$$

Adding the equations, we get: $f(1000)-f(0)=4 \cdot(0+2+4+\cdots+998)+2 \cdot 500=4$. $\frac{998 \cdot 500}{2}+1000=999000$. Then $f(1000)=999001$.

Mom bought four items, the one that cost the least is $\qquad$ yuan.

Note: The translation provided above has already followed the instruction, but if you need the exact format as requested, here it is again:

Mom bought four items, the one that cost the least is $\qquad$ yuan.

Let's construct a right-angled triangle, given the radius $r$ of the circumscribed circle and the bisector of one acute angle: $f$.

---

Translate the above text into English, please retain the original text's line breaks and format, and output the translation result directly.
solution:
I. Solution: Let the sides of the triangle be $a, b, c=2r$, and the two segments created by the angle bisector be $b_1, b_2$. From the two right triangles formed (Figure 1),

$$
a^2 + b^2 = c^2
$$

and

$$
a^2 + b_2^2 = f^2
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_88d55e7c19e32402ac22g-1.jpg?height=336&width=550&top_left_y=388&top_left_x=774)

Figure 1

From the ratio of the segments created by the angle bisector,

$$
\frac{b_2}{b_1} = \frac{a}{c}
$$

but

$$
b_1 + b_2 = b
$$

from these two equations,

$$
b_2 = \frac{ab}{a+c}
$$

Substituting this into the second Pythagorean theorem and using the first one as well,

$$
a^2 + \frac{a^2 b^2}{(a+c)^2} = a^2 \frac{(a+c)^2 + (c^2 - a^2)}{(a+c)^2} = \frac{2a^2 c}{a+c} = f^2
$$

from which:

$$
2ca^2 - f^2 a - f^2 c = 0
$$

Since $a$ is a distance, the positive root will be the solution:

$$
a = \frac{f^2 + \sqrt{f^4 + 8f^2 c^2}}{4c} = \frac{f}{4c} \left(f + \sqrt{f^2 + 8c^2}\right)
$$

or equivalently,

$$
a : f = \left(f + \sqrt{f^2 + 8c^2}\right) : 4c
$$

From this, $a$ can be constructed as follows. First, construct the distance $\sqrt{8}c$, then from the right triangle with legs $f$ and $\sqrt{8}c$, construct the hypotenuse $\sqrt{f^2 + 8c^2}$. Add $f$ to this. From the resulting segment, and using $f$ and $4c$, construct the fourth proportional to get $a$.

With $a$ and $c$ known, the right triangle can be constructed.

The solvability condition is that $f < c$. If this is satisfied, the problem always has one solution.

problem:
SKET $k$ Given: On the parabola $y=x^{2}$, there are three vertices $A, B, C$ of a square. Find: The minimum value of the area of such a square.

Translate the above text into English, please retain the original text's line breaks and format, and output the translation result directly.
solution:
Assume that among the three vertices of the square on the parabola, two are on the right side of the $y$-axis (including the $y$-axis), and let the coordinates of points $A$, $B$, and $C$ be $\left(x_{i}, y_{i}\right), i=1,2,3$. The slope of $BC$ is $k (k > 0)$. Since the points lie on the parabola $y=x^{2}$, we have $y_{1}=x_{1}^{2}, y_{2}=x_{2}^{2}, y_{3}=x_{3}^{2}$. Substituting these into the above equations, we get $x_{3}=k-x_{2}, x_{1}=-\frac{1}{k}-x_{2}$.

Since $|A B|=|B C|$, we have $\sqrt{\left(x_{1}-x_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(y_{1}-y_{2}\right)^{2}}=\sqrt{\left(x_{3}-x_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(y_{3}-y_{2}\right)^{2}}$, so $\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{k^{2}}}\left(x_{2}-x_{1}\right)=\sqrt{1+k^{2}}\left(x_{3}-x_{2}\right)$, which simplifies to $x_{2}-x_{1}=k\left(x_{3}-x_{2}\right)$. Therefore, $\frac{1}{k}+2 x_{2}=k\left(k-2 x_{2}\right)$. From $k^{2}-\frac{1}{k}-(2 k+2) x_{2} \geqslant 0$, we know $k^{3} \geqslant 1$, hence $k>1$. Thus, $x_{2}=\frac{k^{3}-1}{2 k(k+1)}$, and the side length of the square is
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{k^{2}+1}\left(x_{3}-x_{2}\right) & =\sqrt{k^{2}+1}\left(k-2 x_{2}\right)=\sqrt{k^{2}+1}\left[k-\frac{k^{3}-1}{k(k+1)}\right] \\
& =\frac{k^{2}+1}{k} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{k^{2}+1}}{k+1} \geqslant \frac{2 k}{k} \cdot \frac{\frac{k+1}{\sqrt{2}}}{k+1}=\sqrt{2},
\end{aligned}
$$

with equality holding if and only if $k=1$, i.e., when $B$ is at the origin. Therefore, $S_{\max }=(\sqrt{2})^{2}=2$.

problem: After the successful completion of the graduation exams, a charitable foundation awarded a prize among the most outstanding, with the most outstanding receiving a certain amount, the next receiving a bit less than the first, the third receiving the same amount less than the second, and so on; however, in the list of outstanding individuals, the fifth, having left, had their share taken by the third, who received a total of 40 forints for both of them; in the list of outstanding individuals, the ninth also left, and their share was taken by the sixth, who received a total of 30 forints for both of them. How much was the prize for the third, fifth, sixth, and ninth in the list of outstanding individuals?
solution:
The amounts taken by individual students form an arithmetic sequence, where the first term is denoted by $a$ and the common difference by $d$. Thus,

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \text{the 3rd received } a-2d \text{ frt} \\
& \text{the 5th " } a-4d \text{ " } \\
& \text{the 6th " } a-5d \text{ " } \\
& \text{the 9th " } a-8d \text{ " }
\end{aligned}
\]

But according to the conditions, the 3rd and 5th together received 40 frt, and the 6th and 9th received 30 frt. Therefore,

\[
\begin{gathered}
2a - 6d = 40 \\
2a - 13d = 30
\end{gathered}
\]

Subtracting the second equation from the first:

\[
\begin{gathered}
7d = 10 \\
d = \frac{10}{7} \text{ frt}
\end{gathered}
\]

Substituting this value into the first equation,

\[
\begin{gathered}
2a - \frac{60}{7} = 40 \\
a = \frac{170}{7} \text{ frt}
\end{gathered}
\]

Knowing $a$ and $d$, we can write down the amounts taken by each student.

problem:
Given a circle plane $(S)$, its center $(O)$, and radius $(r=\sqrt{a(a+b)})$. There are also two points $(P, Q)$ such that $|P Q| \perp S$ and they lie on $O$. $\overline{O P}=a, \overline{O Q}=a+b$.

Let the circle be the common base of two cones with vertices at $P$ and $Q$. For any point $A$ on the circle, there are two generators. What is the geometric locus of the intersection points of the lines perpendicular to these generators and raised at the vertices of the cones?
solution:
Intersect the cones with the $[A P Q]$ plane. Let the intersection point of the perpendicular lines to the generators in this plane be $M$, and its projection onto $P Q$ be $K$. Since the angles of the perpendicular legs are equal, we have $O A P \varangle = M P K \varangle = \alpha$ and $O A Q \varangle = M Q K \varangle = \alpha + \beta$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_d7dab71942801deea42bg-1.jpg?height=572&width=507&top_left_y=305&top_left_x=798)

From this, it follows that $\triangle A O P \sim \triangle K P M$ and $\triangle A O Q \sim \triangle K Q M$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}
a: r = x: (y + b) \\
(a + b): r = x: y \left| \begin{array}{l}
x r = a y + a b \\
x r = a y + b y
\end{array} \right| y = a \\
x \cdot r = a^2 + a b \\
x = \frac{a(a + b)}{\sqrt{a(a + b)}} = \sqrt{a(a + b)} \quad x = r
\end{gathered}
$$

The geometric locus of the points $M$ is thus a circle whose plane is parallel to $S$, whose center $K$ lies on the line $O P Q$ at a distance $a$ from $Q$, and whose radius is equal to the given $r$.

However, the lines perpendicular to $|P A|$ and $|Q A|$ are not all in the plane $P Q A$, but in planes perpendicular to this plane. Thus, the intersection line of these two planes is $m$, which passes through $M$ and is perpendicular to the plane $[P Q A]$, meaning $m$ is a tangent to the found circle. Any point on $m$ connected to $P$ and $Q$ will give lines perpendicular to $|P A|$ and $|P B|$, respectively.

The sought geometric locus is thus all points in the plane of the found circle that are not inside the circle.

If $P$ and $Q$ are on different sides of $O$, this only changes the distance relationships.

problem:
9.5. At the exchange office, only the following operations can be performed:

1) exchange 2 gold coins for three silver coins and one copper coin;
2) exchange 5 silver coins for three gold coins and one copper coin.

Nikolai had only silver coins. After several visits to the exchange office, he had fewer silver coins, no gold coins appeared, but he got 50 copper coins. By how much did the number of silver coins decrease for Nikolai? Justify your answer. Note that exchanging money at the bank is not an equivalent operation, meaning that with each exchange, the purchasing power of the coins Nikolai had slightly decreased.
solution:
Solution: As a result of each operation, Nikolai acquires exactly 1 copper coin, which means there were exactly 50 operations in total. Of these, some (let's say \(a\)) were of the first type, and the rest \(50-a\) were of the second type. On operations of the first type, Nikolai spent \(2a\) gold coins, and on operations of the second type, he earned \(3(50-a)\) gold coins. Since he has no gold coins left, \(2a = 3(50-a)\), from which \(a = 30\). This means that on operations of the first type, Nikolai received \(30 \cdot 3 = 90\) silver coins, and on operations of the second type, he lost \((50-30) \cdot 5 = 100\) such coins. Thus, the number of silver coins decreased by \(100 - 90 = 10\) coins.

Answer: By 10 coins.
