problem:
Let $x, y$ be positive integers,
$$
x^{2}+y^{2}-2017 x y>0
$$

and not a perfect square. Find the minimum value of $x^{2}+y^{2}-2017 x y$.
solution:
The required minimum value is 2019.
$$
\text { Let } x^{2}+y^{2}-2017 x y=k \text {, }
$$

where $k$ is not a perfect square.
First, prove that $: \geqslant 2019$.
Let $\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)$ be the positive integer solution of equation (1) that minimizes $x_{0}+y_{0}$. Without loss of generality, assume $x_{0} \geqslant y_{0}$.
By the condition, $x_{0}$ is a root of the quadratic equation
$$
x^{2}-2017 y_{0} x+y_{0}^{2}-k=0
$$

Let the other root be $x_{1}$. Then
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x_{0}+x_{1}=2017 y_{0}, \\
x_{0} x_{1}=y_{0}^{2}-k .
\end{array}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we know $x_{1} \in \mathbf{Z}$.
Since $k$ is not a perfect square, then $x_{1} \neq 0$.
If $x_{1}>0$, then
$$
\begin{array}{l}
x_{1}=\frac{y_{0}^{2}-k}{x_{0}}<\frac{y_{0}^{2}}{x_{0}} \leqslant \frac{x_{0}^{2}}{x_{0}}=x_{0} \\
\Rightarrow x_{1}+y_{0}<x_{0}+y_{0},
\end{array}
$$

and $\left(x_{1}, y_{0}\right)$ is also a positive integer solution of equation (1), which contradicts the minimality of $x_{0}+y_{0}$.
Thus, it must be that $x_{1}<0$.
From the system of equations (2), we have
$$
\begin{array}{l}
x_{0} \geqslant 2017 y_{0}+1, y_{0}^{2}-k \leqslant-1 . \\
\text { Hence } k=x_{0}\left(x_{0}-2017 y_{0}\right)+y_{0}^{2} \\
\geqslant\left(2017 y_{0}+1\right) \cdot 1+y_{0}^{2} \geqslant 2019 . \\
\text { Let } x^{2}+y^{2}-2017 x y=2019, \text { then } \\
(x+y)^{2}=2019(x y+1) .
\end{array}
$$

Take $x y+1=2019, x+y=2019$.
Solving, we get $(x, y)=(2018,1)$ or $(1,2018)$.
Therefore, the required minimum value is 2019.
(Fang Tinggang, Chengdu No.7 High School, Sichuan Province, 610041)

problem:
Example 5 Suppose we have a $4 \times 4$ grid where each cell is colored differently. Each cell is filled with either 0 or 1, such that the product of the numbers in any two adjacent cells is 0. How many different ways are there to fill the grid with numbers?

(2007, Korean Mathematical Olympiad)
solution:
【Analysis】Since in any two adjacent cells there is at least one 0, when a cell is filled with 1, all its neighboring cells must be filled with 0. The solution can start from a cell filled with 1.

First, consider which position, when filled with 1, can produce as many 0s as possible. Since the cells in the middle have the most neighbors, we can discuss the number of 1s in the four middle cells.

If there is no 1 in the four middle cells, then the surrounding 12 cells form a circle, and in any two adjacent cells, there is at least one 0. Therefore, we first solve the following local problem.

Lemma 1 If $n$ cells form a circle, and each cell is filled with 0 or 1, such that the product of the numbers in any two adjacent cells is 0, then the number of different filling methods is
$$
b_{n}=F_{n+1}+F_{n-1} \text {. }
$$

The proof can use reduction by recursion, fixing one of the cells. If this cell is filled with 0, then the remaining $n-1$ cells do not form a circle (separated by the cell filled with 0), but form a row. Therefore, to prove Lemma 1, we need to first prove Lemma 2.

Lemma 2 If $n$ cells form a row, and each cell is filled with 0 or 1, such that the product of the numbers in any two adjacent cells is 0, then the number of different filling methods is $a_{n}=F_{n+2}$, where $F_{1}=F_{2}=1, F_{n}=F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}$ is the Fibonacci sequence.

Proof of Lemma 2 Consider the first cell. If this cell is filled with 0, then the remaining $n-1$ cells have $a_{n-1}$ filling methods; if this cell is filled with 1, then its neighboring cell must be filled with 0, and the remaining $n-2$ cells have $a_{n-2}$ filling methods. Therefore,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
a_{n}=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2} . \\
\text { Also, } a_{1}=2=a_{3}, a_{2}=3=a_{5}, \text { thus, } \\
a_{n}=F_{n+2} .
\end{array}
$$

Lemma 2 is proved.
Proof of Lemma 1 Fix one of the cells. If this cell is filled with 0, then the remaining $n-1$ cells form a row, with $a_{n-1}$ filling methods; if this cell is filled with 1, then its two neighboring cells must be filled with 0, and the remaining $n-3$ cells form a row, with $a_{n-3}$ filling methods.
Thus, $b_{n}=a_{n-1}+a_{n-3}=F_{n+1}+F_{n-1}$.
Lemma 1 is proved.
Consider three cases.
(1) If there is no 1 in the four middle cells, then the surrounding 12 cells form a circle, and in any two adjacent cells, there is at least one 0. By Lemma 1, there are
$$
b_{12}=F_{13}+F_{11}=233+89=322
$$

filling methods.
(2) If there is one 1 and three 0s in the four middle cells, then there are 4 ways to fill the 1, and the filling method for 0 is unique. For any of these filling methods, the two neighboring cells of the cell filled with 1 can only be filled with 0, and the common neighboring cell between these two newly filled 0s has 2 filling methods. The remaining 9 cells form a row, and by Lemma 2, there are $a_{9}=F_{11}=89$ filling methods.
Thus, there are $4 \times 2 \times 89=712$ filling methods.
(3) If there are two 1s and two 0s in the four middle cells, then there are 2 ways to fill the two 1s (filling diagonally), and for any of these filling methods, the two cells filled with 1 each have two neighboring cells not filled, which can only be filled with 0, and the common neighboring cell between these two newly filled 0s can be filled with 0 or 1, with 2 filling methods. The remaining six cells form two rows of length 3, and in any two adjacent cells, there is at least one 0. By Lemma 2, each row has $a_{3}=F_{5}=5$ filling methods.
Thus, there are $2^{2} \times 5^{2} \times 2=200$ filling methods.
In total, there are $322+712+200=1234$ filling methods.

problem:
If $p$ and $q$ are positive integers, $\max (p, q)$ is the maximum of $p$ and $q$ and $\min (p, q)$ is the minimum of $p$ and $q$. For example, $\max (30,40)=40$ and $\min (30,40)=30$. Also, $\max (30,30)=30$ and $\min (30,30)=30$.

Determine the number of ordered pairs $(x, y)$ that satisfy the equation

$$
\max (60, \min (x, y))=\min (\max (60, x), y)
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are positive integers with $x \leq 100$ and $y \leq 100$.

## PART B

For each question in Part B, your solution must be well organized and contain words of explanation or justification when appropriate. Marks are awarded for completeness, clarity, and style of presentation. A correct solution, poorly presented, will not earn full marks.
solution:
Solution 1

We consider two cases: $y<60$ and $y \geq 60$.

We use the facts that $\min (a, b) \leq a, \min (a, b) \leq b, \max (a, b) \geq a$, and $\max (a, b) \geq b$. In other words, the minimum of two numbers is less than or equal to both numbers and the maximum of two number is greater than or equal to both numbers.

We also use the fact that if $a \leq b$, then $\min (a, b)=a$ and $\max (a, b)=b$. Note that the case of $a=b$ does not affect these equations.

Case 1: $y<60$

If $y<60$, then $\min (x, y) \leq y$ and $y<60$, so $\min (x, y)<60$.

Since $\min (x, y)<60$, then LS $=\max (60, \min (x, y))=60$.

Also, $\max (60, x) \geq 60$, so since $y<60$, then $\mathrm{RS}=\min (\max (60, x), y)=y$.

Therefore, in the case $y<60$, the equation is satisfied whenever $60=y$, which is never true.

Therefore, there are no ordered pairs $(x, y)$ with $y<60$ that satisfy the equation.

Case 2: $y \geq 60$

If $x<y$, then $\min (x, y)=x$ and so LS $=\max (60, x)$.

If $x<y$, then both 60 and $x$ are no larger than $y$, so the largest of 60 and $x$ is no larger than $y$. In other words, $\max (60, x) \leq y$ and so $\mathrm{RS}=\min (\max (60, x), y)=\max (60, x)$.

If $x<y$, the equation becomes $\max (60, x)=\max (60, x)$ and so is true for every ordered pair $(x, y)$.

If $x \geq y$, then $\min (x, y)=y$ and so $\mathrm{LS}=\max (60, y)=y$ since $y \geq 60$.

If $x \geq y$, then $x \geq 60$ so $\max (60, x)=x$ and so $\mathrm{RS}=\min (x, y)=y$.

If $x \geq y$, the equation becomes $y=y$ and so is true for every pair $(x, y)$.

Therefore, the given equation is satisfied by all pairs $(x, y)$ with $y \geq 60$.

Since $1 \leq x \leq 100$, there are 100 possible values for $x$.

Since $60 \leq y \leq 100$, there are 41 possible values for $y$.

Therefore, there are $100 \times 41=4100$ ordered pairs that satisfy the equation.

## Solution 2

In this solution, we use the facts that if $a \leq b$, then $\min (a, b)=a$ and $\max (a, b)=b$.

We also label as $(*)$ the original equation $\max (60, \min (x, y))=\min (\max (60, x), y)$.

We consider the possible arrangements of the integers $60, x$ and $y$.

There are six possible arrangements. We examine the various pieces of the left and right sides of the given equation for each of these orders, moving from the innermost function out on each side:

$$
\begin{array}{|c||c|c||c|c|}
\text { Case } & \min (x, y) & \mathrm{LS}=\max (60, \min (x, y)) & \max (60, x) & \mathrm{RS}=\min (\max (60, x), y) \\
\hline 60 \leq x \leq y & =x & =\max (60, x)=x & =x & =\min (x, y)=x \\
60 \leq y \leq x & =y & =\max (60, y)=y & =x & =\min (x, y)=y \\
x \leq 60 \leq y & =x & =\max (60, x)=60 & =60 & =\min (60, y)=60 \\
x \leq y \leq 60 & =x & =\max (60, x)=60 & =60 & =\min (60, y)=y \\
y \leq 60 \leq x & =y & =\max (60, y)=60 & =x & =\min (x, y)=y \\
y \leq x \leq 60 & =y & =\max (60, y)=60 & =60 & =\min (60, y)=y
\end{array}
$$

If $60 \leq x \leq y$, then $(*)$ is equivalent to $x=x$, so all $(x, y)$ with $60 \leq x \leq y$ satisfy $(*)$. If $60 \leq y \leq x$, then $(*)$ is equivalent to $y=y$, so all $(x, y)$ with $60 \leq y \leq x$ satisfy $(*)$. If $x \leq 60 \leq y$, then $(*)$ is equivalent to $60=60$, so all $(x, y)$ with $x \leq 60 \leq y$ satisfy $(*)$. If $x \leq y \leq 60$, then $(*)$ is equivalent to $60=y$, so only $(x, y)$ with $y=60$ and $x \leq 60$ satisfy
$(*)$. These $(x, y)$ are already accounted for in the third case.

If $y \leq 60 \leq x$, then $(*)$ is equivalent to $60=y$, so only $(x, y)$ with $y=60$ and $x \geq 60$ satisfy $(*)$. These $(x, y)$ are included in the second case.

If $y \leq x \leq 60$, then $(*)$ is equivalent to $60=y$, so only $y=60$ and $60 \leq x \leq 60$, which implies $x=60$. In this case, only the pair $(60,60)$ satisfies $(*)$ and this pair is already included in the first case.

Therefore, we need to count the pairs of positive integers $(x, y)$ with $x \leq 100$ and $y \leq 100$ which satisfy one of $60 \leq x \leq y$ or $60 \leq y \leq x$ or $x \leq 60 \leq y$.

From these three ranges for $x$ and $y$ we see that $y \geq 60$ in all cases and $x$ can either be less than or equal to 60 or can be greater than or equal to 60 and either larger or smaller than $y$.

In other words, these three ranges are equivalent to the condition that $y \geq 60$.

Therefore, $(*)$ is satisfied by all pairs $(x, y)$ with $y \geq 60$.

Since $1 \leq x \leq 100$, there are 100 possible values for $x$.

Since $60 \leq y \leq 100$, there are 41 possible values for $y$.

Therefore, there are $100 \times 41=4100$ ordered pairs that satisfy the equation.

ANSWER: 4100

problem: 7. [5] A line in the plane is called strange if it passes through $(a, 0)$ and $(0,10-a)$ for some $a$ in the interval $[0,10]$. A point in the plane is called charming if it lies in the first quadrant and also lies below some strange line. What is the area of the set of all charming points?
solution:
Answer: $50 / 3$
Solution: The strange lines form an envelope (set of tangent lines) of a curve $f(x)$, and we first find the equation for $f$ on $[0,10]$. Assuming the derivative $f^{\prime}$ is continuous, the point of tangency of the line $\ell$ through $(a, 0)$ and $(0, b)$ to $f$ is the limit of the intersection points of this line with the lines $\ell_{\epsilon}$ passing through $(a+\epsilon, 0)$ and $(0, b-\epsilon)$ as $\epsilon \rightarrow 0$. If these limits exist, then the derivative is indeed continuous and we can calculate the function from the points of tangency.
The intersection point of $\ell$ and $\ell_{\epsilon}$ can be calculated to have $x$-coordinate $\frac{a(a-\epsilon)}{a+b}$, so the tangent point of $\ell$ has $x$-coordinate $\lim _{\epsilon \rightarrow 0} \frac{a(a-\epsilon)}{a+b}=\frac{a^{2}}{a+b}=\frac{a^{2}}{10}$. Similarly, the $y$-coordinate is $\frac{b^{2}}{10}=\frac{(10-a)^{2}}{10}$. Thus, solving for the $y$ coordinate in terms of the $x$ coordinate for $a \in[0,10]$, we find $f(x)=10-2 \sqrt{10} \sqrt{x}+x$, and so the area of the set of charming points is
$$
\int_{0}^{10}(10-2 \sqrt{10} \sqrt{x}+x) d x=50 / 3 .
$$

problem: The circles $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ (with different radii) touch each other at point $T$. A line $e$ passing through $T$ intersects the circles at points $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$. The intersection of the lines $O_{1} M_{2}$ and $O_{2} M_{1}$ is point $P$. What curve does $P$ trace as the line $e$ rotates around $T$?
solution:
In the task, the role of the two circles is identical and their radii are different, so we can assume that, for example, $k_{2}$ has the larger radius: $r_{1}<r_{2}$.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_f26482df389d77f040adg-1.jpg?height=954&width=1808&top_left_y=241&top_left_x=148)

First, we examine the case when the circles touch each other externally. In this case, $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ subtend $T$, and the radii $0_{1} M_{1}, 0_{2} M_{2}$ are in opposite directions. If one of $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ is on the line $O_{1} O_{2}$, the other is also there, and $P$ does not exist. Otherwise, the quadrilateral $O_{1} M_{1} O_{2} M_{2}$ is a trapezoid where the non-parallel sides $O_{1} M_{2}, M_{1} O_{2}$ are not parallel, since the parallel sides $O_{1} M_{1}, M_{2} O_{2}$ are not equal. Since the first of these two sides is the smaller one, the extensions of the sides $O_{1} M_{1}$ beyond $O_{1}$ intersect, and this is where the point $P$ is. Let the intersection of the line through $P$ parallel to $O_{1} M_{1}$ with $O_{1} O_{2}$ be $O$, which is also on the opposite side of $O_{1} M_{1}$ from $O_{2} M_{2}$. Therefore, the triangles $O_{1} O_{2} M_{1}$ and $O O_{2} P$ are similar,

$$
O P: O_{1} M_{1}=O O_{2}: O_{1} O_{2}=O_{2} P: O_{2} M_{1}
$$

The triangles $P M_{1} O_{1}$ and $P O_{2} M_{2}$ are also similar, so $P M_{1}: P O_{2}=r_{1}: r_{2}$, and thus the common value of the above ratios is

$$
O_{2} P: O_{2} M_{1}=P O_{2}:\left(P O_{2}-P M_{1}\right)=r_{2}:\left(r_{2}-r_{1}\right)
$$

Therefore,

$$
O P=\frac{r_{1} r_{2}}{r_{2}-r_{1}}
$$

and

$$
O O_{2}=\frac{\left(r_{1}+r_{2}\right) r_{2}}{r_{2}-r_{1}}
$$

Because of these, the position of $O$ does not depend on the choice of $e$, and the distance between $P$ and $O$ is also independent of this choice. This means that $P$ lies on the circle centered at $O$ with radius $r=r_{1} r_{2} /\left(r_{2}-r_{1}\right)$. Conversely, if $P$ is any point on this circle, not on the line $O_{1} O_{2}$, but otherwise arbitrary, then the radii $O_{1} M_{1}$ and $O_{2} M_{2}$ of $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$, respectively, which are in the same direction as $O P$ and in the opposite direction of $O P$, respectively, determine points $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ such that the triangles $O_{1} O_{2} M_{1}$ and $O O_{2} P$, as well as the triangles $P M_{1} O_{1}$ and $P O_{2} M_{2}$, are similar, since two of their sides are parallel and their ratios are equal. Thus, $M_{1}$ is on the line $P O_{2}$ and $M_{2}$ is on the line $P O_{1}$, and since $O_{1} M_{1}$ and $O_{2} M_{2}$ are in opposite directions, $M_{1} M_{2}$ passes through $T$. Therefore, any point of the circle centered at $O$ with radius $r$ that is not on the line $O_{1} O_{2}$ belongs to the geometric locus in question.

We now turn to the case where $k_{1}$ touches $k_{2}$ internally (we still assume that $r_{1}<r_{2}$). In this case, $O_{1} M_{1}$ and $O_{2} M_{2}$ are in the same direction, so $P$ and the $O$ determined by it are between them. The triangles $O_{1} O_{2} M_{1}$ and $O O_{2} P$ are still similar, so (1) remains valid, but now $P M_{1} O_{1}$ and $P O_{2} M_{2}$ are on opposite sides of the line $O P$, so from their similarity, instead of (2), it follows that

$$
O_{2} P: O_{2} M_{1}=O_{2} P:\left(O_{2} P+P M_{1}\right)=r_{2}:\left(r_{2}+r_{1}\right)
$$

Therefore, now $r=O P=r_{1} r_{2} /\left(r_{2}+r_{1}\right), O O_{2}=\left(r_{2}-r_{1}\right) r_{2} /\left(r_{2}+r_{1}\right)$, so $P$ traces out the points of the circle centered at $O$ with radius $r$ that are different from the intersection points with $O_{1} O_{2}$.

problem:
## Task 2 - 240512

Roland solved a division problem. He obtained the quotient 36.

To check his result, Roland multiplied the divisor by this quotient. However, he mistakenly read a 1 instead of a 7 in the divisor and obtained the result of this multiplication as 756 instead of the given dividend.

What was the division problem that Roland was supposed to solve?
solution:
During the practice, Roland multiplied the wrong number by 36 and got 756. Since $756 : 36 = 21$, this wrong number was 21. The error occurred because he read a 7 as a 1. The correct number should have been 27.

With this, Roland would have obtained $27 \cdot 36 = 972$ during his practice. This was thus the given dividend. The division problem Roland was supposed to solve was therefore 972 : 27.

problem:
$[$ Modular arithmetic (miscellaneous).] $]$ [ Products and factorials $]$

Can $m!+n!$ end in 1990?
solution:
If both $m$ and $n$ are greater than 3, then $m! + n!$ is divisible by 4 and therefore cannot end in 90.

If $m \leq 3$, then the sum has more than three digits only when $n > 6$, and in that case, $n!$ is divisible by 10, so $m! + n!$ ends in 1, 2, or 6.

## Answer

It cannot.

problem:
## Problem Statement

Calculate the lengths of the arcs of the curves given by equations in a rectangular coordinate system.

$$
y=1+\arcsin x-\sqrt{1-x^{2}}, 0 \leq x \leq \frac{3}{4}
$$
solution:
## Solution

The length of the arc of a curve defined by the equation $y=f(x) ; a \leq x \leq b$ is given by the formula

$$
L=\int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1+\left(f^{\prime}(x)\right)^{2}} d x
$$

Let's find the derivative of the given function:

$$
f^{\prime}(x)=\left(1+\arcsin x-\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\right)^{\prime}=(\arcsin x)^{\prime}-\left(\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\right)^{\prime}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}-\frac{2 x}{-2 \sqrt{1-x^{2}}}=\frac{1+x}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}
$$

Then, using the formula above, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}
L & =\int_{0}^{3 / 4} \sqrt{1+\left(\frac{1+x}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\right)^{2}} d x= \\
& =\int_{0}^{3 / 4} \sqrt{1+\frac{1+x}{1-x}} d x= \\
& =\int_{0}^{3 / 4} \sqrt{\frac{1-x+1+x}{1-x}} d x= \\
& =\int_{0}^{3 / 4} \frac{\sqrt{2} d x}{\sqrt{1-x}}= \\
& =-\sqrt{2} \int_{0}^{\frac{3 / 4}{\sqrt{1-x}}}= \\
& =-\left.\sqrt{2} \cdot 2 \sqrt{1-x}\right|_{0} ^{3 / 4}=-2 \sqrt{2}\left(\sqrt{1-\frac{3}{4}}-1\right)=-2 \sqrt{2}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\sqrt{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

problem: 7.5. In a row, there are 20 free chairs. solution:
Answer. $y=x^{2}+2 x-3$ and $y=x^{2}-3 x+2$.

Solution. Some number $t$ is a root of both quadratic polynomials, so $t^{2}+b t+c=t^{2}+c t+b$, from which $(b-c)(t-1)=0$. Since $b \neq c$ (otherwise the parabolas would coincide), we get that $t=1$. If the parabola $y=x^{2}+b x+c$ intersects the x-axis at points -3 and 1, then by the converse of Vieta's theorem, $b=-(-3+1)=2$, $c=-3 \cdot 1=-3$.

problem: 4. The bisectors of the exterior angles at vertices $A$ and $D$ of trapezoid $\mathrm{ABCD}(\mathrm{AB} \| \mathrm{CD}$) intersect at point $\mathrm{M}$, and the bisectors of the exterior angles at vertices B and C intersect at point $\mathrm{N}$ such that $\overline{\mathrm{MN}}=12 \mathrm{~cm}$. Calculate the perimeter of the trapezoid.
solution:
Solution: According to the given conditions, points $\mathrm{M}$ and $\mathrm{N}$ are equally distant from the bases. This means that points $\mathrm{M}$ and $\mathrm{N}$ lie on a line that contains the midline of the trapezoid. Then $\measuredangle 1 = \Delta 2$.

- by condition; $\Delta 1 = \triangle 3$ as alternate interior angles. It follows that $\triangle \mathrm{AMP}$ is isosceles, so $\overline{\mathrm{PM}} = \overline{\mathrm{PA}} = \overline{\mathrm{PD}}$. Similarly, $\overline{\mathrm{QN}} = \overline{\mathrm{QB}} = \overline{\mathrm{QC}}$.

$\overline{\mathrm{MN}} = \overline{\mathrm{MP}} + \overline{\mathrm{PQ}} + \overline{\mathrm{QN}} = \frac{\overline{\mathrm{AD}}}{2} + \frac{\overline{\mathrm{AB}} + \overline{\mathrm{CD}}}{2} + \frac{\overline{\mathrm{BC}}}{2}$

$= \frac{1}{2}(\overline{\mathrm{AB}} + \overline{\mathrm{BC}} + \overline{\mathrm{CD}} + \overline{\mathrm{DA}}) = \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~L}$.

It follows that $\mathrm{L} = 2 \cdot \overline{\mathrm{MN}} = 2 \cdot 12 = 24$; $\mathrm{L} = 24 \mathrm{~cm}$.

## Task 11/67

Given are two circles $K(A)$ and $K(B)$ with centers $A$ and $B$, respectively, which intersect at $S$ and $S^{\prime}$. $P_{A}$ and $P_{B}$ are points on $K(A)$ and $K(B)$, respectively, such that $S$ lies on the segment $P_{A} P_{B}$.

The geometric locus of the midpoints of all possible segments $P_{A} P_{B}$ is sought.
solution:
Let $S_{A}$ and $S_{B}$ be the endpoints of a diameter of $K(A)$ and $K(B)$, respectively, whose second common endpoint is $S$. Furthermore, let $S_{M}$ be the midpoint of $S_{A} S_{B}$, $P_{A}^{\prime}$ and $P_{B}^{\prime}$ be the intersection points of the tangents at $S$ to $K(B)$ with $K(A)$ and to $K(A)$ with $K(B)$, respectively (see figure).

Then the arc of the circle centered at the midpoint of $S S_{M}$ with radius $\frac{1}{2} S S_{M}$, running from $P_{A}^{\prime} S$ to $P_{B}^{\prime} S$, is the desired geometric locus.

Proof: By the Thales' theorem, $P_{A} S_{A} \perp P_{A} P_{B}$ and $P_{B} S_{B} \perp P_{A} P_{B}$, so $P_{A} S_{A}$ and $P_{B} S_{B}$ are parallel to the perpendicular bisector of $P_{A} P_{B}$. By the intercept theorem, this perpendicular bisector intersects the segment $S_{A} S_{B}$ at $S_{M}$. Therefore, the midpoint of $P_{A} P_{B}$ lies on the Thales' circle over $S S_{M}$.

Since $P_{A} P_{B}$ cannot pass through the triangle $S P_{A}^{\prime} P_{B}^{\prime}$ (in this case, $S$ would lie outside $P_{A} P_{B}$), the part of the Thales' circle lying within this triangle is excluded.

After 20 minutes, Tom was directly above Jerry, and neither of them had completed a full lap. After another 15 minutes, Tom returned to the starting point. After how much

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_23de18cc06162d7c52c3g-1.jpg?height=249&width=514&top_left_y=1423&top_left_x=1402)
time from the start of the run will Tom catch Jerry
solution:
Solution. In the first 20 minutes, Tom runs the larger loop, while Jerry runs the smaller one. In the next 15 minutes, Tom runs the smaller loop. Therefore, Tom's speed is $\frac{4}{3}$ times faster than Jerry's, and the larger loop is $\frac{4}{3}$ times longer than the smaller one.

Let the length of the smaller loop be $m$, then the length of the larger loop is $\frac{4 m}{3}$. Initially, Jerry is ahead of Tom by the length of the larger loop, which is $\frac{4 m}{3}$. In the first 20 minutes, the distance between them is reduced by $\frac{m}{3}$. Since the speeds are constant, this reduction will occur every 10 minutes. To catch up $\frac{4 m}{3}$, Tom needs $20 \cdot 4=80$ minutes.

Answer: in 80 minutes.

problem:
Emílio likes to propose mathematical and animal challenges. He wrote on a piece of paper the following sum:

$$
\begin{array}{rcccc} 
& \mathbf{G} & \mathbf{A} \mathbf{O} \\
+ & \mathbf{P} & \mathbf{U} & \mathbf{A} \\
\hline \mathbf{P} & \mathbf{U} & \mathbf{M} & \mathbf{S}
\end{array}
$$

Emílio said that the sum above represents a correct sum of two numbers, where each letter represents a distinct digit.

a) What is the digit represented by the letter $\mathbf{P}$?

b) What are the digits represented by the letters $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{U}$?

c) What is the number represented by the word PUMAS?
solution:
Solution

a) Since the number PUMAS has five digits, and the numbers GATO and PUMA have only four digits, it is necessarily true that the first digit of the number PUMAS is equal to 1, that is, $\mathbf{P}=1$.

b) To find the value of $\mathbf{U}$, we need to note that there are two possibilities:

$$
\mathbf{G}+1=10+\mathbf{U} \quad \text { or } \quad 1+\mathbf{G}+1=10+\mathbf{U}
$$

Note that the second case can only occur if $\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{U}$ is greater than or equal to 9.

In the first case, we have $\mathbf{G}=9+\mathbf{U}$, which is only possible if $\mathbf{G}=9$ and $\mathbf{U}=0$.

In the second case, $\mathbf{G}=8+\mathbf{U}$, which could only happen if $\mathbf{U}$ were equal to 1 or 0. But $\mathbf{U}$ cannot be equal to 1, since we already have $\mathbf{P}=1$. Thus, the only remaining possibility is $\mathbf{U}=0$ and $\mathbf{G}=8$. But with $\mathbf{U}=0$, it could not be that $\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{U}=10$. Therefore, we should have $\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{U}=9$, which would give us $\mathbf{A}=9$. But this cannot happen either, since we would have $\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{U}=9$. Thus, the second case must be discarded.

We conclude then that the first case holds, that is, $\mathbf{U}=0$ and $\mathbf{G}=9$.

c) From items $a$) and $b$), we already know that $\mathbf{P}=1, \mathbf{G}=9$ and $\mathbf{U}=0$. Therefore, the operation

$$
\begin{array}{rccc} 
& \mathbf{G} & \mathbf{A} \mathbf{O} \\
+ & \mathbf{P} & \mathbf{U} & \mathbf{A} \\
\hline \mathbf{P} & \mathbf{U} & \mathbf{M} & \mathbf{A}
\end{array}
$$

can be rewritten as:

|  | 9 | $\mathbf{A}$ | $\mathbf{T}$ | $\mathbf{O}$ |
| ---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| + | 1 | 0 | $\mathbf{M}$ | $\mathbf{A}$ |
| 1 | 0 | $\mathbf{M}$ | $\mathbf{A}$ | $\mathbf{S}$ |

Thus, it also holds that

| $\mathbf{A}$ | $\mathbf{T}$ | $\mathbf{O}$ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| + | $\mathbf{M}$ | $\mathbf{A}$ |
| $\mathbf{M}$ | $\mathbf{A}$ | $\mathbf{S}$ |

Since $\mathbf{A} \neq \mathbf{M}$, this can only happen if $\mathbf{A}+1=\mathbf{M}$. From this, we have two possibilities:

$$
\mathbf{M}+\mathbf{T}=10+\mathbf{A} \quad \text { or } \quad \mathbf{M}+\mathbf{T}+1=10+\mathbf{A}
$$

(Note that the second case occurs when $\mathbf{O}+\mathbf{A} \geq 10$). Since $\mathbf{A}+1=\mathbf{M}$, the first case gives us $\mathbf{T}=9$, which cannot happen, since we already have $\mathbf{G}=9$.

Thus, we conclude that the second case holds: $\mathbf{M}+\mathbf{T}+1=10+\mathbf{A}$. Since $\mathbf{A}+1=\mathbf{M}$ also holds, we can conclude that $\mathbf{T}=8$. Remembering that $\mathbf{O}+\mathbf{A} \geq 10$, and knowing that $\mathbf{S} \neq 0$ and $\mathbf{S} \neq 1$, we must have $\mathbf{O}+\mathbf{A} \geq 12$.

Since $\mathbf{T}=8$, then:

$$
\mathbf{A} \in\{2,3,4,5,6,7\} \quad \text { and } \quad \mathbf{S} \in\{2,3,4,5,6,7\}
$$

Since $\mathbf{A}+1=\mathbf{M}$, $\mathbf{A}$ cannot be 7, because in that case, we would have $\mathbf{M}=8$, which is impossible, since we already know that $\mathbf{T}=8$.

Thus, indeed, we have:

$$
\mathbf{A} \in\{2,3,4,5,6\} \quad \text { and } \quad \mathbf{S} \in\{2,3,4,5,6,7\}
$$

Since $\mathbf{O}+\mathbf{A} \geq 12$, and $\mathbf{O} \neq \mathbf{A}$, the only choice left is

$$
\mathbf{A}=5 \quad \text { and } \quad \mathbf{O}=7
$$

which also gives us $\mathbf{S}=2$. Furthermore, since $\mathbf{A}+1=\mathbf{M}$, we have $\mathbf{M}=6$.

Thus, the number PUMAS is equal to 10652.

problem:
Ribamko A.V.

In the lower left corner of a $n \times n$ chessboard, there is a knight. It is known that the minimum number of moves it takes for the knight to reach the upper right corner is equal to the minimum number of moves it takes to reach the lower right corner. Find $n$.

#
solution:
Let $n$ be even. In this case, the left lower field has the same color as the right upper one, while the right lower field has a different color. After each move, the knight lands on a field of the opposite color. Therefore, any path from the left lower corner to the right upper one consists of an even number of moves, while the path to the right lower corner consists of an odd number of moves. Consequently, their lengths are different.

: Let $n=4 k+1$. Then, by making moves alternately along the fields of the two lower rows, the knight will reach the right lower corner in $2 k$ moves.

We will show that the path to the right upper corner is longer. Each move shifts the knight by a total of 3 fields horizontally and vertically. Even moving consistently to the right-up, the knight will move a total of $6 k$ fields in $2 k$ moves. The total distance horizontally and vertically from the left lower corner to the right upper one is $2 n-2 = 8 k > 6 k$. Therefore, the shortest path to the right upper field is longer.

Let $n=4 k-1$. Then, the right lower field can be reached in $2 k$ moves as follows: the first move is one field to the right and two up, the second move is one field to the right and two down, and then, as in the previous case, move alternately along the fields of the two lower rows. It is impossible to reach the destination in fewer moves.

Indeed, the knight needs to move $n-1=4 k-2$ cells to the right, and each move can shift it a maximum of two cells to the right. Therefore, the number of moves is at least $2 k-1$. But after $2 k-1$ moves, the knight will land on a field of the opposite color, while in our case, the right lower corner has the same color as the left lower corner, so at least one more move is needed, meaning the number of moves is at least $2 k$.

The maximum total shift to the right and up in $2 k$ moves remains $6 k$. The total distance horizontally and vertically from the left lower field to the right upper one is $2 n-2 = 8 k-4$. For $k>2$, this is greater than $6 k$. For $k=1 (n=3)$, it is easy to check all options and see that this case does not work. However, for $k=2 (n=7)$, both shortest paths consist of four moves, and this is also easy to verify.

## Answer

$n=7$.

problem: 3. Given 10 points in space, where no four points lie on the same plane, connect some of the points with line segments. If the resulting figure contains no triangles and no spatial quadrilaterals, determine the maximum number of line segments that can be drawn.
solution:
Given a simple graph $G$ of order 10 with these 10 points as vertices and the connected line segments as edges. Let the vertices of graph $G$ be $v_{1}, v_{2}, \cdots, v_{10}$, and there are $k$ edges. Use $\operatorname{deg}\left(v_{i}\right)$ to denote the degree of vertex $v_{i}$.
If $\operatorname{deg}\left(v_{i}\right) \leqslant 3$ for $i=1,2, \cdots, 10$, then $k=\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{10} \operatorname{deg}\left(v_{i}\right) \leqslant \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 3=15$; if there exists a vertex $v_{i}$ such that $\operatorname{deg}\left(v_{i}\right) \geqslant 4$, without loss of generality, let $\operatorname{deg}\left(v_{1}\right)=n \geqslant 4$, and $v_{1}$ is adjacent to $v_{2}, v_{3}, \cdots, v_{n+1}$. Thus, there are no edges between $v_{2}, v_{3}, \cdots, v_{n+1}$, otherwise, a triangle would be formed, which is a contradiction. Therefore, there are exactly $n$ edges between $v_{1}, v_{2}, \cdots, v_{n+1}$.
For each $v_{j}(n+2 \leqslant j \leqslant 10)$, $v_{j}$ can be adjacent to at most one of $v_{2}, v_{3}, \cdots, v_{n+1}$ (otherwise, if $v_{j}$ is adjacent to $v_{s}, v_{t}(2 \leqslant s<t \leqslant n+1)$, then $v_{1}, v_{s}, v_{j}, v_{t}$ would form a quadrilateral, which is a contradiction). Thus, there are at most $10-(n+1)=9-n$ edges between $v_{2}, v_{3}, \cdots, v_{n+1}$ and $v_{n+2}, \cdots, v_{10}$.
Among the $9-n$ vertices $v_{n+2}, \cdots, v_{10}$, since there are no triangles, by Turán's theorem (a simple $n$-order graph without triangles has at most $\left[\frac{n^{2}}{4}\right]$ edges), there are at most $\left[\frac{(9-n)^{2}}{4}\right]$ edges. Therefore, the number of edges in graph $G$ is
$$
k \leqslant n+9-n+\left[\frac{(9-n)^{2}}{4}\right] \leqslant 9+\left[\frac{25}{4}\right]=15 .
$$

The graph shown on the right has 15 edges and meets the requirements.
In conclusion, the maximum number of edges is 15.

problem:
$\underline{\text { Ivanov V. }}$.

a) The vertices of a regular 10-gon are painted alternately black and white. Two players play the following game. Each, in turn, draws a segment connecting vertices of the same color. These segments must not have any common points (even endpoints) with previously drawn ones. The player who makes the last move wins. Who wins with correct play: the player starting the game or their partner?

b) The same question for a 12-gon.
solution:
a) The second player can apply a symmetric strategy: each time, draw a segment that is centrally symmetric to the segment drawn by the first player. In this way, he will always have a move, so he cannot lose.

b) Here, the starting player can apply a symmetric strategy: first, he connects the opposite vertices, and then acts according to the strategy described in a).

## Answer

a) Partner; b) starting player.

solution: 1. Let $x$ be a common root, then $x^{2} + a x + 1 = 0$, (1) $x^{2} + x + a = 0$, (2) Subtracting (2) from (1) gives $(a-1) \cdot (x-1) = 0$. If $a=1$, then equations (1) and (2) are identical, in which case the two polynomials have a common root. If $a \neq 1$, then the common root $x=1$, substituting into (1), (2) both yield $a=-2$. Therefore, the required $a=1$ or -2.

## Problem Statement

Calculate the limit of the function:
$\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} \frac{x^{3}-4 x^{2}-3 x+18}{x^{3}-5 x^{2}+3 x+9}$
solution:
## Solution

$\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} \frac{x^{3}-4 x^{2}-3 x+18}{x^{3}-5 x^{2}+3 x+9}=\left\{\frac{0}{0}\right\}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} \frac{(x-3)\left(x^{2}-x-6\right)}{(x-3)\left(x^{2}-2 x-3\right)}=$

$=\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} \frac{x^{2}-x-6}{x^{2}-2 x-3}=\left\{\frac{0}{0}\right\}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} \frac{(x-3)(x+2)}{(x-3)(x+1)}=$

$=\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} \frac{x+2}{x+1}=\frac{3+2}{3+1}=\frac{5}{4}=1 \frac{1}{4}$

problem:
Subject 3. Consider the adjacent angles $\Varangle A O B$ and $\Varangle B O C$, such that their bisectors [OM and $\left[O N\right.$ form an angle of $75^{\circ}$.

a) Determine $m(\Varangle A O B)$ and $m(\Varangle B O C)$ knowing that $3 \cdot m(\Varangle A O B)=2 \cdot m(\Varangle B O C)$.

b) If the ray [OT forms a right angle with the ray [OM such that points $M$ and $T$ are on the same side as point $B$ relative to point $A$. Calculate: $m(\Varangle T O N), m(\Varangle B O N)$ and $m(\Varangle B O T)$ and $m(\Varangle C O T)$.
solution:
## Solution:

a) Let $m(\angle A O B)=\alpha$ and $m(\angle B O C)=\beta$. We have:

$[O M]$ is the bisector of $\angle A O B \Rightarrow m(\angle A O M)=m(\angle M O B)=\frac{\alpha}{2}$;

$[O N]$ is the bisector of $\angle B O C \Rightarrow m(\angle B O N)=m(\angle N O C)=\frac{\beta}{2}$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_06_07_9e90d71b69e1f57c0219g-2.jpg?height=334&width=654&top_left_y=1386&top_left_x=1272)

Since $m(\angle M O N)=75^{\circ}$, we have $\frac{\alpha}{2}+\frac{\beta}{2}=75^{\circ} \Leftrightarrow \alpha+\beta=150^{\circ} \Rightarrow \alpha=150^{\circ}-\beta$, (1).

But $3 \cdot m(\angle A O B)=2 \cdot m(\angle B O C) \Rightarrow 3 \alpha=2 \beta$, (2).

From (1) and (2) we have $3(150^{\circ}-\beta)=2 \beta \Leftrightarrow 450^{\circ}=5 \beta \Leftrightarrow \beta=90^{\circ}$ and $\alpha=150^{\circ}-90^{\circ}=60^{\circ}$.

Thus, $m(\angle A O B)=60^{\circ}$ and $m(\angle B O C)=90^{\circ}$.

b) We have $m(\angle M O T)=90^{\circ}$, from which we get: $m(\angle T O N)=90^{\circ}-[m(\angle N O B)+m(\angle M O B)]=15^{\circ}$;

problem:
Let's consider the curves

$$
\begin{aligned}
& y=-x^{2}+4 \ldots \\
& \text { and } 16 x^{2}+25 y^{2}=400 \ldots
\end{aligned}
$$

when rotated about the $Y$-axis. What volume is cut out from the solid of revolution (1) by the solid of revolution (2)?
solution:
1) The parabola, whose main axis is the $Y$-axis; by rotating the parabola around this, we obtain a rotational paraboloid.

2) The ellipse, one of whose main axes is the $Y$-axis; by rotating it around this, we obtain a rotational ellipsoid.

The parabola touches the ellipse at the point $x=0, y=+4$; in addition, it intersects at two points that are symmetric with respect to the $Y$-axis. For these points,

$$
16 x^{2}+25\left(-x^{2}+4\right)^{2}=400, \quad \text { or } \quad x^{2}\left(25 x^{2}-184\right)=0
$$

Here, $x^{2}=0$ indicates that the two curves touch at the point $x=0, y=+4$.

For the intersection points $P_{1}, P_{2}$, we have $25 x^{2}-184=0$,

$$
x^{2}=\frac{184}{25}, \quad x= \pm \frac{2}{25} \sqrt{46}
$$

Thus,

$$
y=-\frac{184}{25}+4=-\frac{84}{25}=-3.36
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_72d87c077498e73b9d2cg-1.jpg?height=385&width=414&top_left_y=797&top_left_x=842)

The volume in question consists of two parts: one part is the slice of the paraboloid cut by a plane perpendicular to the $Y$-axis through points $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$; the other part is the smaller slice of the ellipsoid cut by the same plane. The volume of the first part, if $x^{2}$ is expressed from the equation of the parabola,

$$
\begin{gathered}
K_{1}=\int_{-3.36}^{+4} x^{2} \pi \cdot d y=\pi \int_{-3.36}^{4}(4-y) d y= \\
=\pi\left[4 y-\frac{y^{2}}{2}\right]_{-3.36}^{4}= \\
=\pi\left(16-8+4 \cdot 3.36+\frac{3.36^{2}}{2}\right)= \\
=\pi(8+13.144+5.6448)=27.0848 \pi
\end{gathered}
$$

The volume of the second part (if $x^{2}$ is expressed from the equation of the ellipse),

$$
\begin{gathered}
K_{2}=\int_{-4}^{-3.36} x^{2} \pi d y=\pi \int_{3.36}^{4}\left(25-\frac{25}{16} y^{2}\right) d y=\pi\left[25 y-\frac{25}{48} y^{3}\right]_{3.36}^{4}= \\
=\pi\left[100-\frac{25}{48} 64-25 \cdot 3.36+\frac{25}{48} 3.36^{3}\right]= \\
=\pi\left(100-\frac{100}{3}-84+\frac{84}{48} \cdot 3.36^{2}\right)=-\pi(-17.3333+3.5 \cdot 5.6448)= \\
=2.4235 \pi \\
K=K_{1}+K_{2}=27.0848 \pi+2.4235 \pi \sim 29.51 \pi \quad \text { volume units. }
\end{gathered}
$$

B. Major Pál (Ref. rg. VIII. o. Csurgó).

problem:

$$
\frac{p q+p^{p}+q^{q}}{p+q}
$$

can take, where $p$ and $q$ are both prime numbers.

Answer: The only possible integer value is 3 .
solution:
Solution: If both $p$ and $q$ are odd, then the numerator is odd while the denominator is even. Since an even number never divides an odd number, this does not lead to an integer value. Hence we can assume that one of our primes is even and therefore equal to 2 . Since the expression is symmetric in $p$ and $q$, we can assume without loss of generality that $q=2$.

Substituting $q=2$, it remains to determine all integer values taken by the expression

$$
\frac{2 p+p^{p}+4}{p+2}=\frac{2(p+2)+p^{p}}{p+2}=2+\frac{p^{p}}{p+2}
$$

In order for this to be an integer, we must have that $p+2$ is a divisor of $p^{p}$. But since $p$ is prime, the only positive divisors of $p^{p}$ are $1, p, p^{2}, \ldots, p^{p-1}$ and $p^{p}$. If $p>2$, then we have

$$
p2$ the expression $p+2$ never divides $p^{p}$ and we don't get integer values. The only case remaining is $p=q=2$, making the original expression equal to 3 .

problem: 3. Given a $101 \times 101$ grid, all cells of which are painted white. It is allowed to choose several rows and repaint all cells in these rows to black. Then, choose exactly the same number of columns and repaint all cells in these columns to the opposite color (i.e., white to black, and black to white). What is the maximum number of black cells that the grid can contain after this operation?
solution:
Answer: 5100.

Solution. Let $k$ rows be repainted first, then $k$ columns. After the first stage of repainting, each column will contain $k$ black and $101-k$ white cells. Since $101-k$ columns will remain untouched, the total number of black cells in these columns will be $k(101-k)$. In each of the repainted columns, there will be $101-k$ black cells, so the total number of black cells in these columns will be $(101-k)k$. Therefore, the total number of black cells is $f(k) = 2k(101-k)$. It is clear that the graph of the function $f(x) = 2x(101-x)$ is a parabola with branches pointing downwards. This means that the maximum value of the function $f(x) = 2x(101-x)$ is achieved at the point $a = \frac{101}{2}$, and the function increases up to this point and then decreases. Therefore, for any integer $k$, $f(k) \leq f(50)$ for $0 \leq k \leq 50$ and $f(k) \leq f(51)$ for $51 \leq k \leq 101$. It remains to note that $f(50) = f(51) = 5100$.

Remark. The analysis of the behavior of the function $f(x)$ can be conducted using the derivative. From the fact that the maximum value of the function $f(x)$ is achieved at the point $a = \frac{101}{2}$, it does not follow that the function $f(k)$ (for integer $k$) must achieve its maximum value at one of the nearest integer points to $a$. Although this is true for our function, in general, there is a counterexample. For a valid conclusion, a reference to monotonicity is needed.

Comment. Only the answer - 1 point.

In the solution, an explicit formula for the number of black cells (in terms of $k$) is obtained - no less than 3 points.

An unproven conclusion that the maximum value is $f(50)$ or $f(51)$ - no more than 4 points.

problem: For a given triangle, construct three circles of equal radius that pass through one point, and each side of the triangle is tangent to exactly two of the circles.
solution:
Let's consider the problem as solved. Let the vertices of the triangle be $A, B, C$, and the centers of the circles be $P, Q, R$. Consider one side of the triangle. The two (different) circles tangent to this side also touch one other side of the triangle each, so the centers of these two circles are in the same half-plane as $A B C$ with respect to the line of the side. Since the radii of the circles are equal, the line connecting the centers of the circles is parallel to the selected side. This is true for each side, so the $P Q R$ triangle is similar to the $A B C$ triangle. The common point of the three circles is equidistant from $P, Q, R$, so this point is the center of the circumcircle of the $P Q R$ triangle.

We can solve the problem by constructing a similar diagram and then appropriately scaling it down. This can be done as follows. Draw circles of equal radius around each vertex of the $A B C$ triangle, passing through the center of the circumcircle of the triangle. For each pair of circles, draw the common tangent that does not intersect the third circle. The three tangents form a triangle similar to the $A B C$ triangle, and the circles touch the sides of this triangle as required by the problem. Finally, consider the similarity transformation that maps this triangle to the $A B C$ triangle. This transformation maps the circles to the circles we need to construct.

Remarks: 1. Since the two mentioned triangles are "parallel" similar, they are also centrally similar, and it is easy to see that the center of similarity is the intersection of the internal angle bisectors. The reason we had to choose the common tangent of two circles that does not intersect the third circle is that we use the word "side" in the sense of "segment", and this ensures that the six points of tangency are definitely points on the sides. We also see that the problem always has a solution.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_a2f9f9603f9dbaf9abf7g-1.jpg?height=539&width=483&top_left_y=931&top_left_x=802)

1. Figure
2. If the word "side" in the problem statement is replaced with "side line", then in constructing the similar diagram, any of the two common tangents of any two circles can be considered, and thus the tangents can form 2-3 different similar triangles. One of these 8 solutions is shown in Figure 1. Here, the circles centered at $P$ and $Q$ do not touch the $A C$ and $B C$ sides, but their extensions. In this case, the center of similarity is the intersection of the internal angle bisector at $C$ and the external angle bisectors at the other two vertices. If $A B C$ is a right triangle, then in addition to the aforementioned 8 solutions, the circles can also be constructed such that two of them are tangent to each other. One of these four solutions is shown in Figure 5.
3. Returning to our original problem, the question arises whether there are any other solutions among the more general solutions mentioned in point 2, where all points of tangency fall on the sides (or their extensions). Figures 2 and 3 show that if the $A B C$ triangle is equilateral, then at least two solutions are possible. In the case shown in Figure 3, when constructing the similar diagram, any of the common tangents of any two circles can be chosen to intersect the third circle.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_a2f9f9603f9dbaf9abf7g-1.jpg?height=414&width=460&top_left_y=2078&top_left_x=819)

2. Figure

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_a2f9f9603f9dbaf9abf7g-2.jpg?height=409&width=442&top_left_y=121&top_left_x=820)

3. Figure

We will show that if the $A B C$ triangle is not equilateral, then the problem has exactly one solution, and if the triangle is equilateral, then only the two solutions mentioned above exist. For this, we need to examine the cases mentioned in point 2 individually. Our statement is easily verifiable in every case where one of the common tangents used to construct the triangle does not intersect the circle it does not touch; the details are left to the reader.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_a2f9f9603f9dbaf9abf7g-2.jpg?height=1554&width=686&top_left_y=850&top_left_x=703)

5. Figure

Suppose, however, that there are three circles $k_{1}, k_{2}$, and $k_{3}$ of equal radius passing through a point and touching the sides $A C$ and $A B$, $B C$ and $A B$, and $A C$ and $B C$ respectively, and also intersecting the sides $B C$, $A C$, and $A B$. We can assume, for example, that $B C \leq A C \leq A B$. Scale down the circles $k_{i}$ from $C$ such that the resulting circles $k_{1}^{\prime}, k_{2}^{\prime}, k_{3}^{\prime}$ are such that $k_{3}^{\prime}$ is exactly the incircle of the $A B C$ triangle (Figure 4). Let the centers of $k_{1}^{\prime}, k_{2}^{\prime}$, and $k_{3}^{\prime}$ be $O_{1}, O_{2}$, and $O$; let the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to the line $O O_{1}$ be $T$, and finally, let $A^{\prime}$ be the point where $k_{3}^{\prime}$ touches the side $B C$. Since $k_{1}^{\prime}$ touches the side $A C$, we have

$$
O O_{1} \leq O T
$$

As we have already seen, the triangle $\mathrm{O}_{1} \mathrm{O}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ is similar to $A B C$, and the ratio of similarity is $\frac{r}{R}$, where $r$ is the radius of the incircle of the $A B C$ triangle, and $R$ is the radius of the circumcircle of the triangle. Thus (denoting the sides and angles of the triangle in the usual way)

$$
O O_{1}=\frac{r}{R} b
$$

The right triangles $O T C$ and $O A^{\prime} C$ are congruent, as they share the hypotenuse $O C$ and one of their acute angles is $\frac{\gamma}{2}$; therefore

$$
O T=C A^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2}(a+b-c),
$$

From (1), (2), and (3) we get

$$
\frac{r}{R} b \leq \frac{1}{2}(a+b-c)
$$

or (denoting the area of the triangle by $t$)

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{a+b-c}{b} \geq \frac{2 r}{R}=\frac{4 t}{a+b+c} \cdot \frac{4 t}{a b c} \\
a+b-c \geq \frac{16 t^{2}}{a c(a+b+c)}=\frac{(-a+b+c)(a-b+c)(a+b-c)}{a c}
\end{gathered}
$$

Thus

$$
a c \geq(a+(c-b)) \cdot(c+(b-a))
$$

Since by assumption $c \geq b \geq a$, it follows from the above inequality that $c-b=0=b-a$; hence the $A B C$ triangle is equilateral.

problem: Problem 3. Numbers from 1 to 50 are written on cards. Can these cards be placed into 11 bags (so that each bag contains at least one card) in such a way that the product of the numbers on the cards in each bag is divisible by 9?
solution:
Answer: No.

Solution. Suppose the opposite: let it be possible to distribute the cards into eleven bags so that the condition is met.

For the product of the numbers on the cards in some bag to be divisible by 9, it is necessary and sufficient that one of the two conditions is met:

- among the numbers on the cards in this bag, there is at least one that is divisible by 9;
- among the numbers on the cards in this bag, there are at least two that are divisible by 3.

Among the numbers from 1 to 50, exactly five are divisible by 9 (these are the numbers $9, 18, 27, 36, 45$). Therefore, at least six bags do not contain numbers divisible by 9. These bags must contain at least two numbers that are divisible by 3 but not by 9. Thus, there must be at least 12 numbers that are divisible by 3 but not by 9. However, in the range from 1 to 50, there are exactly 11 such numbers $(3, 6, 12, 15, 21, 24, 30, 33, 39, 42, 48)$. Contradiction.

## Criteria

## 0 points. Only the answer without proof.

1 point. The work contains the observation that among the numbers in a bag, there should be one divisible by 9 or two divisible by 3, but there is no further progress.

3 points. A logically flawed but conceptually correct solution. Here is a sketch of such a potential solution: "There are exactly 5 numbers divisible by 9, which we place in 5 bags; there are 11 other numbers divisible by 3, which we place in 5 bags, two in each, and one number is left over. In total, 10 bags, but we need 11. Therefore, it is impossible." A logically correct solution should lead to a contradiction for any potential way to distribute the numbers; a logically flawed solution relies on a specific way to distribute the cards into bags, which seems optimal to the author for some reason.

4 points. Any complete and correct solution.

problem: In the triangle $A B C$, we draw the line $D E$ parallel to the base through the midpoint of the height $B B_{1}$. How does the area of the triangle $B D E$ compare to the area of the trapezoid $A D E C$?
solution:
Let the area of triangle $B D E$ be denoted by $t_{1}$, the area of trapezoid $A D E C$ by $t_{2}$, and the area of triangle $A B C$ by $t$. Then,

$$
t_{1}=\frac{B B_{1}}{4} D E=\frac{B B_{1}}{8} A C=\frac{t}{4}
$$

and

$$
t_{2}=t-t_{1}=\frac{3}{4} t
$$

thus

$$
t_{1}: t_{2}=1: 3
$$

(Andor Vilcsek, Eger.)

The problem was also solved by: Baján A., Bauer E., Dénes M., Dőry V., Erdős V., Fried E., Gotléb I., Grünwald Gy., Klein G., Lendvai D., Neumann F., Neumann L., Rosenberg E., Schlesinger R., Schnabel L., Sichermann F., Spitzer L., Steiner L., Stern S., Szántó L., Szilárd V., Viola R., Weinberger Gy., Wellis E.

problem: 2255 $\underset{\star}{\star \star}$ Find the value of $10 \cot (\operatorname{arccot} 3+\operatorname{arccot} 7+\operatorname{arccot} 13+\operatorname{arccot} 21)$.
solution:
Let $a_{n}=1+n+n^{2}$, then $a_{1}=3, a_{2}=7, a_{3}=13, a_{4}=21$. We will first prove a formula:
$$
\operatorname{arccot}\left(1+n+n^{2}\right)=\arctan (n+1)-\arctan n
$$

In fact, let $\alpha=\arctan (n+1), \beta=\arctan n$. Then $0<\beta<\alpha$, $0<\alpha-\beta<\frac{\pi}{2}$. Also,
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \cot [\arctan (n+1)-\arctan n]=\cot (\alpha-\beta) \\
= & \frac{1+\tan \alpha \cdot \tan \beta}{\tan \alpha-\tan \beta}=\frac{1+(n+1) \cdot n}{(n+1)-n} \\
= & 1+n+n^{2} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,
$$
\operatorname{arccot}\left(1+n+n^{2}\right)=\arctan (n+1)-\arctan n \text {. }
$$

Let $\theta=\operatorname{arccot} 3+\operatorname{arccot} 7+\operatorname{arccot} 13+\operatorname{arccot} 21$. By formula (1) we get
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\operatorname{arccot} 3=\arctan 2-\arctan 1, \operatorname{arccot} 7=\arctan 3-\arctan 2, \\
\operatorname{arccot} 13=\arctan 4-\arctan 3, \operatorname{arccot} 21=\arctan 5-\arctan 4 .
\end{array}
$$

Adding the above four equations, we get $\theta=\arctan 5-\arctan 1$. Thus,
$$
\begin{aligned}
& 10 \cot (\operatorname{arccot} 3+\operatorname{arccot} 7+\operatorname{arccot} 13+\operatorname{arccot} 21) \\
= & 10 \cot \theta=10 \cot (\arctan 5-\arctan 1) \\
= & 10 \cdot \frac{1+5 \cdot 1}{5-1}=15 .
\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
For what values of $c$ do the following equations have solutions?

$$
\text { a) } x+\left[\frac{x}{2}\right]=c ; \quad \text { b) } x-\left[\frac{x}{2}\right]=c
$$

If there are solutions, how many solutions are there, and what are the solutions?
solution:
Graphically, we obtain the solution of the given equations by plotting the left side and intersecting it with the line $y=c$ representing the right side.

The $[x / 2]$ term on the left side is a step function, constant over intervals of 2 units, with jumps of 1 unit at even $x$ values. Therefore, the graph of the left side of our equations is obtained by interrupting the line $y=x$ at every integer abscissa value of $2k$ and shifting the segment between abscissas $2k$ and $2k+2$ (including the left endpoint but not the right) by $k$ units in the $y$ direction.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_e249fcf36b102f744371g-1.jpg?height=477&width=330&top_left_y=412&top_left_x=884)

Figure 1

Thus, the image of the left side of equation (a) over the half-closed interval $[2k, 2k+2)$ on the $x$-axis has ordinates satisfying $3k \leq x + \left[\frac{x}{2}\right] < 3k + 2$, and over the next interval $[2k+2, 2k+4)$, the ordinates satisfy $3k + 3 \leq x + \left[\frac{x}{2}\right] < 3k + 5$. Therefore, the values $3k + 2 \leq y < 3k + 3$ do not belong to the range. If $c$ is such a value, i.e., if

$$
\left[c - 3\left[\frac{c}{3}\right]\right] = 2
$$

then equation (a) has no solution; otherwise, it has one solution. Specifically, if $3k \leq c < 3k + 2$, then, since the abscissas of the points on the graph segment are $k$ units smaller than their ordinates, the intersection point is given by

$$
x = c - k = c - \left[\frac{c}{3}\right]
$$

(Validity condition in another form:

$$
\left[c - 3\left[\frac{c}{3}\right]\right] = 0 \quad \text{or} \quad 1.
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_e249fcf36b102f744371g-1.jpg?height=485&width=575&top_left_y=1557&top_left_x=756)

Figure 2

For equation (b), similarly,

$$
\text{if } 2k \leq x < 2k + 2
$$

then $\quad k \leq x - \left[\frac{x}{2}\right] < k + 2$,

and if $2k + 2 \leq x < 2k + 4$,

$$
\text{then } \quad k + 1 \leq x - \left[\frac{x}{2}\right] < k + 3,
$$

which means the left side takes the values

$$
k + 1 \leq c < k + 2
$$

in both intervals. According to this, every real value is taken exactly twice, and the equation has two solutions for any $c$. The abscissa of the intersection point of the graph and the line $y=c$ is $k$ units larger in interval (1) and $k + 1$ units larger in interval (2) than the ordinate, and according to (3), $k = [c] - 1$, so the solutions are:

$$
x_1 = c + [c] - 1, \quad \text{or} \quad x_2 = c + [c].
$$

problem:
Shapovalov A.V.

One hundred seats of a carousel are arranged in a circle at equal intervals. Each is painted yellow, blue, or red. Seats of the same color are placed consecutively and numbered $1,2,3, \ldots$ clockwise. The blue seat № 7 is opposite the red seat № 3, and the yellow seat № 7 is opposite the red seat № 23. Find how many yellow, blue, and red seats there are on the carousel.
solution:
Between the 3rd and 23rd red seats, there are 19 seats, so there are also 19 seats between the 7th blue and the 7th yellow. These are the first six yellow seats, and thus, 19-6=13 blue seats with numbers greater than 7. From this, we find that the total number of blue seats is $7+13=20$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_73983c7cc26f0024f238g-08.jpg?height=895&width=807&top_left_y=499&top_left_x=111)

Traversing half a circle clockwise from the 3rd red seat to the 7th blue seat, we pass (not counting these two) (100-2):2=49 seats. Six of them are blue, and the remaining 49-6=43 are red. Therefore, the total number of red seats is $3+43=46$. The number of yellow seats is $100-20-46=34$.

## Answer

Yellow: 34, Blue: 20, Red: 46.

problem: 12.192. Given two sides $a$ and $b$ of a triangle and the bisector $l$ of the angle between them. Find this angle.
solution:
Solution.

Let $B D$ be the bisector of $\triangle A B C, B D=l, B C=a, A B=b$ (Fig. 12.59), $\angle A B C=\alpha$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_3edb7be591bff54ce350g-0941.jpg?height=462&width=624&top_left_y=76&top_left_x=366)

Then $\angle A B D=\angle C B D=\frac{\alpha}{2}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& S_{\triangle A B C}=S_{\triangle A B D}+S_{\triangle C B D} \Rightarrow \frac{a b}{2} \sin \alpha=\frac{a l}{2} \sin \frac{\alpha}{2}+\frac{b l}{2} \sin \frac{\alpha}{2} \Leftrightarrow 2 a b \sin \frac{\alpha}{2} \cos \frac{\alpha}{2}= \\

problem: 6. (10 points) Person A and Person B work together on a project, which can be completed in several days. If Person A completes half of the project alone, it will take 10 days less than if Person A and Person B work together to complete the entire project; if Person B completes half of the project alone, it will take 15 days more than if Person A and Person B work together to complete the entire project. How many days will it take for Person A and Person B to complete the entire project together? $\qquad$ days.
solution: 【Solution】Solution: Let's assume that it takes $x$ days for person A and person B to complete the entire project together, then person A alone needs $x-10$ days to complete half of the project, and person B alone needs $x+15$ days to complete half of the project. Person A alone needs $2(x-10)$ days to complete the entire project, and person B alone needs $2(x+15)$ days to complete the entire project. Therefore, $\frac{1}{2(x-10)}+\frac{1}{2(x+15)}=\frac{1}{x}$, solving this equation yields $x=60$. Therefore, the answer is 60.

problem:
## 37. International Conference

Four French, two representatives from the Republic of Ivory Coast, three English and four Swedes gathered at a conference to discuss forestry issues. The conference participants from the same country initially sat next to each other on a bench with 13 seats during the opening ceremony, and later, during the working sessions, at a round table with 13 seats.

In how many different ways can the conference participants sit next to each other in each of these two cases?
solution:
37. The number of ways in which 4 French people can sit next to each other on a bench is 4!; representatives from Ivory Coast can be arranged in 2! ways; the English - in 3! ways, and the Swedes - in 4! ways.

From this, we get that the number of ways in which all 13 people can sit on a bench, given that the order of the national delegations is fixed, is

$$
4! \cdot 2! \cdot 3! \cdot 4! = 6912
$$[^23]

The number of ways in which the 4 national delegations can be arranged among themselves on a bench is 4!

Therefore, the total number of possible arrangements of 13 people on a bench is

$$
4! \cdot 6912 = 165888
$$

The number of ways in which the national delegations can be arranged around a round table is, obviously, not 4!, but 3!. Therefore, the total number of possible arrangements of 13 people around a round table is

$$
3! \cdot 6912 = 41472
$$

Explanation. Let's denote the delegations participating in the conference with letters: F - French, C - Ivory Coast, E - English, S - Swedes. The possible arrangements of the delegations around a round table are: FCES, FCSE, FCEC, FSEC, FSCC, FSEC.

The total number of such arrangements is 6, or 3!. On a bench, we have 4 times more arrangements, since, for example, ECF and FSEC are two different orders of arrangement of the delegations, while around a round table, such two arrangements are no longer distinguishable from each other.

& =7 \pi+\Delta_{C_{R}} \operatorname{Arg}\left(1-\frac{2}{z^{6}}-\frac{5}{z^{7}}\right) \rightarrow 7 \pi \quad \text { as } \quad R \rightarrow \infty

from which

Since $u \neq 0$, the application of the argument principle is valid ( $Q_{7}(z)$ has no zeros on the imaginary axis). This line is a straight line (Fig. 13). The vector $w=Q_{7}(z)$ makes a turn in the negative direction by $\pi$ radians. Therefore,

$$

and

problem:
Four houses are located at the vertices of a convex quadrilateral. Where should a well be dug so that the sum of the distances from it to the four houses is the smallest?

#
solution:
Suppose that the desired point does not lie on one of the diagonals and use the triangle inequality.

## Solution

Let the houses be located at the vertices of a convex quadrilateral $A B C D$, the diagonals $A C$ and $B D$ of which intersect at point $O$. Suppose that the well is located at some point $M$, different from $O$. Then

$$
A M + C M \geqslant A C, \quad B M + D M \geqslant B D
$$

and at least one of these inequalities is strict. Therefore,

$$
A M + C M + B M + D M > A C + B D = A O + C O + B O + D O,
$$

i.e., the sum of the distances to the vertices of the quadrilateral $A B C D$ from point $O$ is less than from any other point.

## Answer

At the intersection of the diagonals of the quadrilateral.

problem: 11. (20 points) Find the equation of the locus of the center of an equilateral triangle inscribed in the parabola $y^{2}=2 p x$.
solution:
11. Let the parabola $y^{2}=2 p x$ inscribe an equilateral triangle with the coordinates of its three vertices being $P_{i}\left(2 p t_{i}^{2}, 2 p t_{i}\right)(i=1,2,3)$, and the center of the triangle be $M(x, y)$. Then
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x=\frac{2}{3} p\left(t_{1}^{2}+t_{2}^{2}+t_{3}^{2}\right), \\
y=\frac{2}{3} p\left(t_{1}+t_{2}+t_{3}\right) .
\end{array}\right.
$$

Assume $\triangle P_{1} P_{2} P_{3}$ is in a counterclockwise direction.
Then $\overrightarrow{P_{1} P_{3}}=\overrightarrow{P_{1} P_{2}}\left(\cos \frac{\pi}{3}+\mathrm{i} \sin \frac{\pi}{3}\right)$.
Thus $2 p\left(t_{3}^{2}-t_{1}^{2}\right)+2 p\left(t_{3}-t_{1}\right) \mathrm{i}$
$$
=\left[2 p\left(t_{2}^{2}-t_{1}^{2}\right)+2 p\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right) \mathrm{i}\right] \mathrm{e}^{\frac{\pi}{3} \mathrm{i}} \text {. }
$$

By equating the real parts, we get
$$
\begin{array}{l}
2 t_{3}^{2}-t_{1}^{2}-t_{2}^{2}=-\sqrt{3}\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right) \\
\Rightarrow\left(2 t_{3}^{2}-t_{1}^{2}-t_{2}^{2}\right)\left(t_{2}+t_{1}\right)=-\sqrt{3}\left(t_{2}^{2}-t_{1}^{2}\right) .
\end{array}
$$

Similarly, by equating the imaginary parts, we get
$$
\sqrt{3}\left(t_{2}^{2}-t_{1}^{2}\right)=2 t_{3}-t_{1}-t_{2} \text {. }
$$

From equations (3) and (4), we have
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\left(2 t_{3}^{2}-t_{1}^{2}-t_{2}^{2}\right)\left(t_{2}+t_{1}\right)=-\left(2 t_{3}-t_{1}-t_{2}\right) \\
\Rightarrow\left(3 t_{3}^{2}-t_{1}^{2}-t_{2}^{2}-t_{3}^{2}\right)\left(t_{2}+t_{1}\right) \\
\quad=-\left(3 t_{3}-t_{1}-t_{2}-t_{3}\right) .
\end{array}
$$

Substituting equations (1) and (2) into the above equation, we get
$$
\left(t_{3}^{2}-\frac{x}{2 p}\right)\left(\frac{3 y}{2 p}-t_{3}\right)=\frac{y}{2 p}-t_{3} \text {. }
$$

Similarly,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\left(t_{1}^{2}-\frac{x}{2 p}\right)\left(\frac{3 y}{2 p}-t_{1}\right)=\frac{y}{2 p}-t_{1}, \\
\left(t_{2}^{2}-\frac{x}{2 p}\right)\left(\frac{3 y}{2 p}-t_{2}\right)=\frac{y}{2 p}-t_{2} .
\end{array}
$$

Thus, $t_{1}, t_{2}, t_{3}$ are the roots of the equation
$$
t^{3}-\frac{3 y}{2 p} t^{2}-\left(1+\frac{x}{2 p}\right) t+\left(\frac{y}{2 p}+\frac{3 x y}{4 p^{2}}\right)=0
$$

By Vieta's formulas, we have
$$
\begin{array}{l}
t_{1} t_{2}+t_{2} t_{3}+t_{3} t_{1}=-\left(1+\frac{x}{2 p}\right) . \\
\text { Also, } t_{1}^{2}+t_{2}^{2}+t_{3}^{2}+2\left(t_{1} t_{2}+t_{2} t_{3}+t_{3} t_{1}\right) \\
=\left(t_{1}+t_{2}+t_{3}\right)^{2},
\end{array}
$$

Thus $9 y^{2}=2 p x-8 p^{2}$.

Inside a cylinder lie two spheres of radius $r$ and one sphere of radius $\frac{3r}{2}$ such that each sphere touches the other two and the lateral surface of the cylinder, and the first two equal spheres touch the bottom base, while the third sphere touches the top base of the cylinder. Find the radius of the base of the cylinder if its height is $4r$.

#
solution:
Through the centers $A$ and $B$ of spheres with radius $r$, we draw a plane $\alpha$ perpendicular to the axis of the cylinder. Let $C^{\prime}$ be

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { the projection on this plane of the center } C \text { of a sphere with radius } \frac{\frac{3}{2} r}{} \text {. Then } \\
& C C^{\prime}=4 r-r-\frac{3}{2} r=\frac{3}{2} r, A C^{\prime}=\sqrt{A C^{2}-C C^{\prime 2}}=\sqrt{\left(r+\frac{3}{2} r\right)^{2}-\left(\frac{3}{2} r\right)^{2}}=2 r .
\end{aligned}
$$

Let the radius of the base of the cylinder be $R$. In the cross-section of the cylinder by the plane $\alpha$, we get a circle of radius $R$ with center $O$, two circles of radius $r$ with centers $A$ and $B$, touching each other at some point $E$ and

the circles of the cross-section, as well as a circle of radius $\frac{3}{2} r$ with center $C^{\prime}$, touching the circle of the cross-section internally at some point $D$, and $A B=r+r=2 r$ and $A C^{\prime}=B C^{\prime}=2 r$. Since the line of centers of two
touching circles passes through their point of contact, and $O A=O B=R-r$ and $C^{\prime} A=C^{\prime} B=2 r$, the points $O, E$, $C^{\prime}$, and $D$ lie on the same line, and $E O+O C^{\prime}=C^{\prime} E$ and $C^{\prime} E$ is the height of an equilateral triangle with side $2 r$. Then

$$
\begin{gathered}
O E=\sqrt{O A^{2}-A E^{2}}=\sqrt{(R-r)^{2}-r^{2}}=\sqrt{R^{2}-2 r R}, \\
C^{\prime} E=\frac{2 r \sqrt{3}}{2}=\frac{r \sqrt{3}}{2}, O C^{\prime}=O D-D C^{\prime}=R-\frac{3}{2} r . \\
\text { Therefore, we get the equation } \\
\sqrt{R^{2}-2 r R}+R-\frac{3}{2} r=\frac{r \sqrt{3}}{2}, \\
\text { from which we find that } \\
R=\frac{3 r(7+4 \sqrt{3})}{4(2 \sqrt{3}+1)}=\frac{3(17+10 \sqrt{3})}{44} r .
\end{gathered}
$$

## Answer

$\frac{3(17+10 \sqrt{3})}{44} r$

problem: [ Law of Sines ] [ Law of Cosines ] In triangle $A B C$, medians $A N$ and $C M$ are drawn, $\angle A B C=120^{\circ}$. The circle passing through points $A, M$ and $N$ also passes through point $C$. The radius of this circle is 7. Find the area of triangle $A B C$.
solution:
Prove that the given triangle is isosceles, find $A N$, and to find the sides of the given triangle, apply the Law of Cosines to triangle $A B N$.

## Solution

By the theorem of the midline of a triangle, $M N \| A C$, so $A M N C$ is a trapezoid. Since the trapezoid is inscribed in a circle, it is isosceles. Since $A B=2 \cdot A M=2 \cdot C N=B C$, the triangle $A B C$ is also isosceles, so $\angle B A C=\angle B C A=30^{\circ}$.

If $R$ is the radius of the circle, then

$$
A N=2 R \cdot \sin \angle A C N=2 R \cdot \sin 30^{\circ}=R=7
$$

Let $C N=A M=x$. Then $A B=B C=2 x$. By the Law of Cosines in triangle $A B N$, we have:

$$
A N^{2}=A B^{2}+B N^{2}-2 \cdot A B \cdot B N \cdot \cos 120^{\circ} \text{, or } 49=4 x^{2}+x^{2}+2 x^{2}
$$

From this, we find that $x^{2}=7$. Therefore,

$$
S_{\triangle \mathrm{ABC}}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot A B \cdot B C \cdot \sin \angle A B C=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 x \cdot 2 x \cdot \sin 120^{\circ}=2 x^{2} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=x^{2} \sqrt{3}=7 \sqrt{3}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_aa2960437c2efca8c53fg-36.jpg?height=343&width=878&top_left_y=2032&top_left_x=590)

## Answer

$7 \sqrt{3}$.

problem:
\section*{Problem 3 - 111213}

All non-negative real numbers \(k\) are to be specified for which the polynomial \(f(x)=(x+1)^{4}-(k x)^{2}\)

a) has exactly one,

b) has exactly two distinct,

c) has exactly three pairwise distinct

d) has exactly four pairwise distinct,

e) has no

real root(s).
solution:
}

Let \(k=0\). Then \(f(x)=(x+1)^{4}\); the function \(f(x)\) thus has exactly one real root, namely \(x=-1\).

Let \(k>0\). Then we can perform the following transformation: \(f(x)=g(x) h(x)\) with

\[
\begin{aligned}
g(x) & =(x+1)^{2}+k x=\left(x+1+\frac{k}{2}\right)^{2}-\left(\frac{k^{2}}{4}+k\right) \\
& =\left(x+1+\frac{k}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{k^{2}}{4}+k}\right)\left(x+1+\frac{k}{2}-\sqrt{\frac{k^{2}}{4}+k}\right) \\
h(x) & =(x+1)^{2}-k x=\left(x+1+\frac{k}{2}\right)^{2}-\left(\frac{k^{2}}{4}-k\right)
\end{aligned}
\]

For the further transformation of \(h(x)\), we distinguish the following cases:

Case 1: \(\frac{k^{2}}{4}-k>0\) or, equivalently due to \(k>0\), \(k>4\). Then:

\[
h(x)=\left(x+1+\frac{k}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{k^{2}}{4}-k}\right)\left(x+1+\frac{k}{2}-\sqrt{\frac{k^{2}}{4}-k}\right)
\]

and \(h(x)\) thus has exactly two distinct real roots.

Case 2: \(\frac{k^{2}}{4}-k=0\) or, equivalently due to \(k>0\), \(k=4\). Then: \(h(x)=\left(x+1+\frac{k}{2}\right)^{2}\) and \(h(x)\) thus has exactly one root.

Case 3: \(\frac{k^{2}}{4}-k<0\) or, equivalently due to \(k>0\), \(k<4\). Then:

\[
h(x)=\left(x+1+\frac{k}{2}\right)^{2} - \left(\frac{k^{2}}{4}-k\right) > 0
\]

and \(h(x)\) thus has no roots.

In all three cases, \(g(x)\) has exactly two distinct roots due to \(k>0\). Furthermore, none of the roots of \(g(x)\) is equal to any of the roots of \(h(x)\) (if such exist); for if a number \(x_{0}\) were both a root of \(g(x)\) and a root of \(h(x)\), then for it:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \left(x_{0}+1\right)^{2}+k x_{0}=\left(x_{0}+1\right)^{2}-k x_{0} \\
& \left(x_{0}+1\right)^{2}+k x_{0}=0
\end{aligned}
\]

From (1), it would follow due to \(k>0\) that \(x_{0}=0\), and this contradicts (2).

Thus, for \(k=0\) we get the answer a), for \(k>0\) in Case 1 the answer d), in Case 2 the answer c), in Case 3 the answer b), and never the answer e).

problem: Exercise 2. A farmer plants carrots in a garden, which initially contains 33 carrots. On some days, the farmer picks one carrot and plants 7. On other days, a very obsessive rabbit comes and eats exactly 4 carrots. Is it possible that one day there will be no carrots left in the garden?
solution:
Solution to Exercise 2: We first notice that on the days the farmer passes, the number of carrots increases by 6, while on the days the rabbit passes, it decreases by 4. In all cases, the parity of the total number of carrots remains unchanged. Since there is an odd number of carrots in the field at the start, this remains the case at the end of each day. Let's modify the following curves.

$$
x^{2}+y^{2}=225, \quad x^{2}-30 x+y^{2}+189=0
$$

Construct the common tangents of these curves, determine the equations of these tangents and the coordinates of the points of tangency.
solution:
The first equation is the equation of a circle whose center $O$ is the origin of the coordinate system, and whose radius is 15. The second equation can also be written as:

$$
(x-15)^{2}+y^{2}=6^{2}
$$

We see that this equation is for a circle whose radius is $6$, and the distance of its center $O_{1}$ from $O$ is 15. Since the circles intersect each other, there are only two common tangents. Let the points of tangency be $M$ and $M_{1}$, and the tangents be $m$ and $m_{1}$, respectively, and the intersection point of the tangents be $A$; the angles $\angle AOM = \angle AO_{1}m = \alpha$, then

$$
\left(O O_{1}+O_{1} A\right): O_{1} A=O M: O_{1} m
$$

from which, after substituting the values,

$$
O_{1} A=10
$$

The equation of the tangent is of the form

$$
x \cos \alpha+y \sin \alpha=O M
$$

but

$$
\cos \alpha=\frac{O M}{O A}=\frac{3}{5} \text { and } \sin \alpha=\frac{M A}{O A}=\frac{4}{5}
$$

so the equation of the tangent is

$$
3 x+4 y=75
$$

The equation of the other tangent is

$$
3 x-4 y=75
$$

Since the points of tangency satisfy both the circle and the tangent equations, the coordinates of point $M$ are the solutions of $x^{2}+y^{2}=225$ and equation (2), which are $(9,12)$ and thus the coordinates of point $M_{1}$ are $(9,-12)$; the coordinates of point $m$ are the solutions of equations (1) and (2), which are $\left(18 \frac{3}{5}, 4 \frac{4}{5}\right)$ and thus the coordinates of point $m_{1}$ are $\left(18 \frac{3}{5},-4 \frac{4}{5}\right)$.

(Kázmér Smodics, Veszprém.)

problem: Annipanni and Boribon take turns writing digits next to each other, moving from left to right on the paper. Annipanni starts with a digit other than 0. They continue the game until they have a 100-digit number. Boribon wins if the resulting number, when divided by 11, leaves a remainder of 5; otherwise, Annipanni wins. Both of them are very good at math. Which of them will win the game?
solution: Solution. Annipanni has a winning strategy, for example, the following: start with a 5, and then always write down the number that Boribon wrote previously. No matter what $b$ digit Boribon adds at the end, a remainder of 5 cannot be formed. The reason for this is that a number's remainder when divided by 11 is the same as the remainder when the alternating sum of its digits (with the units digit being positive, the tens digit negative, etc.) is divided by 11. Thus, within the number, adjacent identical digits receive opposite signs, so they sum to zero. Therefore, the remainder of the 100-digit number when divided by 11 is the same as the remainder of $b-5$ when divided by 11. This can never be 5, because otherwise $(b-5)-5=b-10$ would be divisible by 11, which is clearly impossible since $0 \leq b \leq 9$ implies $-10 \leq b-10 \leq-1$.

problem:
[ Constructions (other).]

Given three points $A, B, C$. Through point $A$, draw a line such that the sum of the distances from points $B$ and $C$ to this line is equal to a given segment.
solution:
Suppose the required line $l$ is constructed. Consider two cases.

Line $l$ intersects segment $B C$. Draw a perpendicular from point $B$ to line $l$, and draw a line from point $C$ parallel to $l$. Let $A^{\prime}$ be the intersection point of the two drawn lines. Triangle $A^{\prime} B C$ is a right triangle. In it, the hypotenuse $B C$ and the leg $A^{\prime} B$ are known. From this, the following construction follows. Construct triangle $A^{\prime} B C$, and then draw line $l$ perpendicular to $B A^{\prime}$. If line $l$ intersects segment $B A^{\prime}$, then this line is the required one. Line $l$ does not intersect segment $B C$. Complete triangle $A B C$ to form parallelogram $A B A^{\prime} C$. The sum of the distances from points $B$ and $C$ to line $l$ is equal to the distance from point $A^{\prime}$ to line $l$. From this, the following construction follows. Construct a right triangle $A A^{\prime} H$ with the given hypotenuse $A A^{\prime}$ and leg $A^{\prime} H$, the length of which is equal to the length of the given segment. If line $l=A H$ does not intersect segment $B C$, then this line is the required one.

problem:
Does there exist a positive rational number $q$ such that $q^{3}-10 q^{2}+q-2021=0$?

(Hint: $45^{2}=2025$)
solution:
Let's write $q=\frac{a}{b}$ with $a, b$ coprime. We then have $\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{3}-10\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)-2021=0$, and by multiplying by $b^{3}$, we get $a^{3}-10 a^{2} b+a b^{2}-2021 b^{3}=0$. Thus, $b\left(-10 a^{2}+a b-2021 b^{2}\right)=-a^{3}$, so $b \mid a^{3}$. Since $a$ and $b$ are coprime, we have $b=1$.

Similarly, $a\left(a^{2}-10 a b+b^{2}\right)=2021 b^{3}$, so $a \mid 2021$. Since $2021=2025-4=45^{2}-2^{2}=(45-2)(45+2)=43 \cdot 47$, we have $q=a=1,43,47,2021$. Conversely, none of these values work (We check manually for 1, and for the other values, $q^{3}$ is much too large for the other terms to cancel it out).

problem: Example: 510 people go to the bookstore to buy books, it is known that: (1) each person bought three types of books; (2) any two people have at least one book in common. How many people at most bought the book that was purchased by the fewest people?
solution:
Let the number of people who bought the most popular book be $x$. Among the 10 people, person A bought three books. Since the other 9 people each have at least one book in common with A, and $9 \div 3=3$, it follows that among A's three books, the most popular one must have been bought by at least 4 people, so $x \geqslant 4$.
If $x=4$, then each of A's three books was bought by 4 people.
Similarly, each of the other 9 people's books was also bought by 4 people.
Therefore, the total number of books bought by the 10 people should be a multiple of 4, i.e., 4 | 30, which is a contradiction. Thus, $x \geqslant 5$.
When $x=5$, let $A_{i}$ represent different books. The scenario where the most popular book is bought by exactly 5 people can be represented by the following sets: $\left\{A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}\right\},\left\{A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{6}\right\},\left\{A_{2}, A_{3}, A_{4}\right\},\left\{A_{1}, A_{4}, A_{6}\right\},\left\{A_{1}, A_{4}, A_{5}\right\}$, $\left\{A_{2}, A_{4}, A_{5}\right\},\left\{A_{1}, A_{3}, A_{5}\right\},\left\{A_{2}, A_{5}, A_{6}\right\},\left\{A_{3}, A_{5}, A_{6}\right\},\left\{A_{3}, A_{4}, A_{6}\right\}$.

problem: 13.50. Three runners $A, B$ and $C$ are running on parallel tracks at constant speeds. At the initial moment, the area of triangle $A B C$ is 2, and after 5 seconds, it is 3. What could it be after another 5 seconds?
solution: 13.50. Let at the initial moment, i.e., at $t=0, \overrightarrow{A B}=\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\overrightarrow{A C}=\boldsymbol{w}$. Then at moment $t$ we get $\overrightarrow{A B}=\boldsymbol{v}+t(\boldsymbol{b}-\boldsymbol{a})$ and $\overrightarrow{A C}=\boldsymbol{w}+t(\boldsymbol{c}-\boldsymbol{a})$, where $\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{c}$ are the velocity vectors of runners $A, B$ and $C$. Since vectors $\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{c}$ are parallel, then $(\boldsymbol{b}-\boldsymbol{a}) \vee(\boldsymbol{c}-\boldsymbol{a})=0$, and therefore, $|S(A, B, C)|=|\overrightarrow{A B} \vee \overrightarrow{A C}| / 2=|x+y t|$, where $x$ and $y$ are some constant numbers. Solving the system $|x|=2,|x+5 y|=3$, we get two solutions, giving for the dependence of the area of triangle $A B C$ on time $t$ the expressions $|2+(t / 5)|$ and $|2-t|$. Therefore, at $t=10$ the area can take the values 4 and 8.

problem:
5. Determine the largest natural number $n$ such that there exists a sequence of $n$ real numbers with the following properties:

(i) the sum of any three consecutive terms of the sequence is positive,

(ii) the sum of any five consecutive terms of the sequence is negative.
solution:
Solution.

For $n=6$ there exists a sequence with the desired property, for example,

$$
3,-5,3,3,-5,3
$$

(5 points)

Note. A student who finds only an example for $n=5$, (e.g., $-1-13-1-1$) gets 2 points.

Assume there exists a sequence of length $n \geqslant 7$ with the desired property. Choose any 7 consecutive terms

$$
a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, a_{4}, a_{5}, a_{6}, a_{7}
$$

of such a sequence. Then, due to (i), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { (1) }\left\{\begin{array}{l}
a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}>0 \\
a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}>0 \\
a_{3}+a_{4}+a_{5}>0 \\
a_{4}+a_{5}+a_{6}>0 \\
a_{5}+a_{6}+a_{7}>0
\end{array}\right. \\
& \text { (2) }\left\{\begin{array}{l}
a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}+a_{5}<0 \\
a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}+a_{5}+a_{6}<0 \\
a_{3}+a_{4}+a_{5}+a_{6}+a_{7}<0
\end{array}\right.
\end{aligned}
$$

By adding the inequalities (1),

$$
\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}\right)+\left(a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\right)+\left(a_{3}+a_{4}+a_{5}\right)+\left(a_{4}+a_{5}+a_{6}\right)+\left(a_{5}+a_{6}+a_{7}\right)>0
$$

By adding the inequalities (2),

$$
\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}+a_{5}\right)+\left(a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}+a_{5}+a_{6}\right)+\left(a_{3}+a_{4}+a_{5}+a_{6}+a_{7}\right)<0
$$

The left sides of these inequalities are equal, leading to a contradiction.

(10 points) Therefore, $n<7$. The longest such sequence has 6 terms.
